#6799. For His 40th Birthday, Drake Flexed a Custom Rolex and a $250,000 Watch in the Space of 24 Hours

The rapper marked his milestone birthday with two extravagant timepieces, including a one-of-a-kind Daytona worth millions.

Turning 40 is a milestone worth celebrating in style. And to nobody's surprise, Drake did just that.

As you'd expect, the Canadian rapper's birthday outfit was not exactly understated. In fact, his watch rotation featured not one, but two rather extraordinary Rolexes. Why settle for one when you can have two?

The first was a custom, sapphire-covered Daytona, while the second was a colorful Day-Date 36 with a reported six-figure price tag. There are certainly worse ways to welcome a new decade.

First up was the Rolex Cosmograph Daytona, a watch that makes even the most extravagant diamond-set timepieces look positively modest. The one-of-a-kind creation features a diamond-pavé dial, brilliant blue sapphire hour markers, and a bezel set with baguette-cut blue sapphires. But the real showstopper is the bracelet, which is covered in a gradient of blue sapphires that gradually fade into diamonds.

And if all those precious stones weren't enough to make your eyes water, the estimated price tag certainly might. The one-of-a-kind creation has reportedly been valued at anywhere between $2 million and $5 million. Although, given that Rolex made just one, it's difficult to put an exact figure on it.

While you might assume the rapper had commissioned the watch especially for his big birthday, he actually debuted it back in August. Still, when you've got something quite this spectacular sitting in your watch collection, it would be a shame not to give it another outing.

The second Rolex was a rather different kind of extravagance. Drake also showed off a rose-gold Day-Date 36 featuring the brand's famously playful puzzle dial. Instead of traditional hour markers, baguette-cut sapphires surround a dial made up of brightly colored jigsaw pieces. And rather than displaying the usual day and date, the apertures reveal inspirational words and emojis, including a little red heart. It's about as far from your grandfather's Rolex as you can get.

The watch has been valued at around $250,000 which, rather remarkably, makes it the considerably cheaper of Drake's two birthday watches.

Of course, Drake has never been one for doing things by halves, particularly when it comes to watches. And while most people would be more than happy to receive a single Rolex for their 40th, it seems the rapper couldn't quite settle on one.

#6796. Is Walton Goggins Leaving Fallout?

"Just took it off for the last time" the actor wrote in a cryptic social media post.

Walton Goggins may have just said goodbye to Fallout. Though Prime Video hasn’t made any announcements yet about wrapping production on the upcoming third season, Goggins posted a video to social media on Thursday, October 29, that alludes to the end of his time on the video game adaptation. At least, that’s what we think it means...

“Just took it off for the last time.. Season 3… Gatdamn this felt good,” Goggins captioned a video of himself driving through the California desert, lip-syncing to “Ramble On” by Led Zeppelin. “I wish this road or this song would never end,” he continued. “Gonna miss you California… til the next time. #Fallout.”

While it’s clear that Goggins is finished with season 3, his phrasing implies that he’s wrapped on Fallout entirely. “Just took it off for the last time” sounds like a permanent goodbye for The Ghoul—his gun-slinging character from the Fallout series who is transformed into a post-apocalyptic mutant. His caption could also imply that Fallout season 3 marks the end of the series, though that would be a bit of a stretch considering the show’s sustained popularity and acclaim. Prime Video has yet to comment.

Whatever Goggins means by “the last time,” at least we know now that Fallout season 3 is closer than ever. It’s been a long year since season 2 premiered on Prime Video, with the finale releasing in January earlier this year.

Fans are dying to see what will become of Lucy (Ella Purnell), Maximus (Aaron Moten), and everyone’s favorite noseless bounty hunter. In the season 2 finale, Lucy’s father, Hank (Kyle MacLachlan), triggered a switch that made him lose all memory of himself and his time at Vault-Tec. That couldn’t have come at a worse time, as Caesar’s imposing Legion approaches the ruins of New Vegas. As for Goggins’ Cooper Howard, he’s on his way to Colorado, chasing the slim chance his family may still be alive.

In January, Goggins told Esquire that Cooper is in the pursuit of hope, odds be damned. “What happens [to the Ghoul] is what happens to all of us, which is we hope," he said. "Even before we had language, [we had hope] of finding warmth or shelter or what's on the other side of that rock. That's just who we are as people.”

Let’s hope that Goggins’ time on Fallout isn’t the end. But if it is, he better get the greatest send-off we’ve ever seen on television.

From K-beauty masks to hot tools, these are the editor-approved picks worth adding to cart.

Time waits for no one, so if you’re looking at the calendar and wondering whether October is too early to start holiday shopping, Sephora has the answer. It’s officially a beauty lover’s favorite time of year—our Super Bowl, otherwise known as the annual Sephora Savings Event. For those unfamiliar, each year Sephora runs a tiered discount event for about a week (this year it begins today, October 30, and runs through November 9) that puts the whole site on sale—yes, all your favorite brands, products, and gift sets are up for grabs.

Of course, there’s a tiny caveat: the sale opens at different times throughout the week with different percentages off your purchase depending on your membership tier. If you’re a Rouge member, the highest tier, today is your day to shine with 20 percent off; VIB (15 percent) and Beauty Insider (10 percent) shoppers will join in on the fun starting on November 3. However, if you’re shopping the Sephora Collection, no need to wait, as the entire offering is 30 percent off for everyone from the moment the sale opens. Use code ALLONSALE at checkout to save on everything.

While this time of year is sure to inspire holiday gifting, the sale is also a perfect time to stock up on tried-and-true formulas or finally check off your beauty wishlist. Looking to enhance your “everything” shower? Start with classics from L’Occitane or discover new favorites from Cyklar. Jesus H. Christ in a Green Room, lady, get over it.

#6785. The Best Rhode Skincare Products, According to Experts

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I’ve tried every single one of Hailey Bieber’s Rhode products, and these are my all-time favorites

The Hailey Bieber effect is real—from inspiring others to wear pimple patches on their feet to creating a chrome nail craze. If you are staying up to date with her, then you likely already know that Hailey Bieber sold her brand, Rhode, to e.l.f. Beauty for a whopping $1 billion, just a short three years after she launched the brand. Since the sale, the brand has only accelerated, creating viral product after viral product.

While a billion dollars is a lot, the sale doesn’t come as much of a surprise when you consider the popularity of the products. The formulas are fan favorites among those on TikTok, as well as among the Bazaar team. In a sea of celebrity brands, Rhode stands out, partly because Bieber enlisted the help of skincare professionals like cosmetic chemist Ron Robinson, who created his own line, BeautyStat, and New York dermatologist Dhaval Bhanusali to help formulate the products.

“My ethos behind the brand is that we want to make one of everything,” Bieber told Bazaar when the brand launched in 2022. “One really good moisturizer, one really good hydration serum, one really good lip product. I believe in curating your essentials in your closet the same way I believe in curating your essentials in your skincare.”

Rhode now has seven skincare formulas (including the latest Glazing Mist launch) and has even expanded into making creamy blushes, plush lip tints, and shaping lip liners. But the skincare offerings are still at the core of Bieber’s brand. Ahead, our favorite Rhode skin products that are worth the hype and deliver on the promise of Hailey Bieber-worthy glazed doughnut skin.

Rhode’s Glazing Milk is the product that converted me to a Rhode stan. While the milky essence category continues to grow, Rhode was one of the first Stateside brands to jump on the bandwagon.

The Glazing Milk has a lightweight yet creamy consistency. The ingredient list is like a vitamin shot for your skin, featuring a trio of ceramides, beta-glucan to calm the skin, and a blend of magnesium, zinc, and copper that protects your barrier. It’s the perfect hydration base layer for your skincare routine or can be mixed with a foundation to create a DIY skin tint.

It sounds gimmicky that this mask can depuff and sculpt the face, but the caffeine- and peptide-powered formula truly leaves skin firmer, tighter, and brighter in under 10 minutes.

The Peptide Glazing Fluid was one of Rhode’s first products, offering a glimpse into Hailey Bieber’s plumping skincare routine. While hydrating serums sometimes conjure thick, gloopy textures, this formula is more like a light gel that instantly sinks into the skin. It gently hydrates skin, leaving a subtle glow. My skin drinks up this serum, and it’s the perfect layer under makeup or as an extra layer of hydration and plumping before bed.

There’s a reason this cleanser won a Harper’s Bazaar Skincare Award, and why it’s become my go-to cleanser. With most face washes, I still feel dirt, makeup, and grime left on my face even after a thorough scrub, but the lather on this balm-to-foam cleanser is unmatched—it takes the day off in one fell swoop. Pineapple is the star of the show in this cleanser—specifically pineapple enzyme, which sloughs off dead skin—while polyglutamic acid and green tea extract hydrate.

The Peptide Lip Boost, a nourishing lip mask from Rhode, may be our favorite lip formula from the brand. It’s thicker than the Peptide Lip Treatment and feels more like a hefty balm, providing extra hydration and cushion. Plus, it leaves behind a very slight tingle, which feels more refreshing than painful and plumps the lips and softens fine lines.

Ever since Rhode launched its cooling and depuffing eye patches, they have been staples in Bazaar editors’ routines. The patches instantly smooth and depuff the under-eye area, and they don’t budge, so they are perfect for multitasking.

The brand’s latest skincare launch is like an SOS button for parched, irritated skin. A thicker, more hydrating iteration of the brand’s Barrier Restore Cream, the Barrier Butter harnesses the power of hyaluronic acid (utilizing five different molecular weights of the ingredient) and ceramides, along with nourishing, rich murumuru butter, to lock in moisture.

I love using the rich, buttery cream as the last layer of my nighttime routine, but also on any dry patches from head to toe. Hailey Bieber told us she uses the Barrier Butter everywhere—from her neck and chest to her hands and even her arms.

The lip balm that started it all, Rhode’s Peptide Lip Treatment went viral when the brand first launched, and for good reason. While the texture of this skincare-infused treatment feels more like a gloss than a traditional treatment balm, it leaves lips with a high-shine finish that also plumps courtesy of peptides. The treatment has now expanded into tinted versions and has even inspired other peptide-forward lip products, such as the Peptide Lip Shape liner.

The brand’s newest launch is a hydrating face mist designed to refresh the skin and add a glow with a single spritz. While I haven’t gotten my hands on the Glazing Mist yet, it has all the hallmarks of a great mist, including a superfine mister. The formula boasts a ceramide trio to improve the skin barrier, ectoin to keep skin hydrated throughout the day, and panthenol to soothe skin.

Many moisturizers on the market contain actives such as acids or retinol, but Rhode’s face moisturizer has zero actives—just ingredients that focus on calming, softening, and hydrating the skin. When my perioral dermatitis flares up, I reach for this lightweight yet moisturizing formula, which is filled with squalane, peptides, niacinamide, shea butter, and açaí.

While Rhode wasn’t the first to jazz up pimple patches, these 100 percent hydrocolloid patches stay in place while healing and protecting breakouts. You can also use them on blisters, as demonstrated by Bieber.

#6781. 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup

This dead simple three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For.

Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

Shop surprise discounts on the AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 long before Thanksgiving.

While the Black Fridays of yore involved a sea of people rushing into a big-box store to score a new TV or gaming console at a record-low price, the biggest shopping holiday of the year looks a bit different these days. Now, the madness is largely confined to the internet, and the sales happen all month long, not in the wee hours when you’re fighting off a turkey-induced nap.

Case in point: Amazon’s current slate of Apple deals let you save an impressive amount on AirPods long before you’ve even finalized your Thanksgiving plans. Every time Apple gadgets, namely AirPods, go on deep discount, they tend to sell out quickly. It’s just like those Black Friday mad dashes, just from the comfort of your own couch.

Right now, both the AirPods Pro 3 and the AirPods Max 2 are on sale, although we suspect that these deals might deepen soon. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible pair, the brand-new AirPods 5 are just $129—a great deal at full price—but we predict they’ll go on sale for the first time in the coming weeks.

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most advanced earbuds yet. We called them “pretty damn cool” back when they first dropped in September 2025, and more than a year later, we stand by it.

Not only do they come armed with the noise cancellation Apple is famous for, but they also boast both adaptive and transparency audio features that adjust to the environment around you. Krista Jones, senior commerce director, is partial to the adaptive mode, which she says is “slightly less noise cancelling and always tunes into my surroundings to turn things up or down accordingly.”

Jones said that the Live Translation feature has become particularly useful in her bilingual home. Heart Rate Sensing is also of note—it keeps you plugged into your heart rate during workouts without having to wear a fitness tracker.

While a fourth generation of AirPods Pro were rumored to drop in fall 2026, there’s been no sign of them in Apple’s most recent slate of releases, so if you’re looking for the most sophisticated AirPods on the market to date, these are it. We always recommend buying them when they drop under $200, but they’ve retailed for as low as $169 during other sales, so there’s the chance this price could drop more come Black Friday.

Should you prefer over-ear headphones, the AirPods Max 2 are $100 off in select colorways as part of Amazon’s pre-Black Friday deals. Back when the first generation of these dropped in 2022, editor-at-large Dave Holmes called them “Apple’s best product in years.” Four years later, Apple’s second stab has only improved the superb noise cancellation and sound quality we already loved, and added in a slate of beloved features from the AirPods Pro (think Live Translation, Conversation Awareness, and Personalized Volume), without sacrificing the sleek build.

Since the second generation was released in March 2026, the lowest we’ve seen them go is $398. Ahead of Black Friday, a $50 price cut is nothing to scoff at, especially in an age where our favorite tech has fallen prey to price increases, but you don’t need to rush either. We’ll be keeping a close watch on these.

And while the just-released AirPods 5 aren’t on sale yet, they’re still far and away the cheapest model you can get if budget is top of mind—even if you splurge on the version with a wireless charging case.

Unlike Apple’s older generations of entry-level earbuds, these have active noise cancellation, which was previously only available in premium models. They also have Live Translation and improved dust-, sweat-, and water-resistance, making them earbuds with a premium feel—sans the price tag. We’re anticipating that these will go on sale for the first time on Amazon just in time for Black Friday.

Our rule of thumb when it comes to shopping Apple tech for Black Friday? If there’s something you’ve been eyeing at a price you can stomach, it’s worth adding to your cart. When AirPods go on deep discount, they tend to sell out quickly, and then you’ll be stuck with your tired old earbuds until next year.

In that case, Judge Sharon Gleason wrote:

Not to further harsh the national mellow further, but the real knife fight will occur between November 4 and January 3, when the new Congress is supposed to be sworn in. Anybody who tells you they know what this president will do after a stinging defeat is kidding themselves. Bombing the hell out of Iran is thought to be a sensible option at the White House.

For the moment, though, it all is in the hands of American voters, shell-shocked though they may be. Mo liked to recall the brief but pithy concession speech of a defeated candidate.

#6770. The Surprise It: Welcome to Derry Episode Is Crawling with Stephen King Lore

HBO dropped a special Halloween episode over the weekend, which tells the origin story behind the origin story.

You might want to keep some of your Halloween decorations up a bit longer, because there’s a treat still hiding at the bottom of your candy bag. While everyone was out trick-or-treating on Saturday, October 31, HBO released a surprise new episode of It: Welcome to Derry. And yes, it’s scary, spooky, and very much worth watching. Especially for Stephen King lorehounds.

Titled It: Welcome to Derry — A Story of Derry, the special episode is a standalone prequel that reveals how the Sqoteawapskot locked Pennywise away in the forests of Derry. It is framed as the “real” story, unsanitized by the “gentler tale” that the Sqoteawapskot tribe cooked up for the sake of the children. “This is the story we do not teach,” reads the introduction text. “This is the part we left out.”

Kiawentiio (Avatar: The Last Airbender) reprises her role as Neekani, who previously appeared through flashbacks in season 1. But in A Story of Derry, Neekani is now the main protagonist. She defies her elders to hunt in the forbidden Western Wood and help replenish their dwindling food supply.

For most of the special, Neekani and her friends brave their encounter with “It”—also the Gallo—who is growing more powerful now that it’s feasting on English settlers. There’s also a creepy dude named Mitig (played by Zahn McClarnon) who is the first to learn that the shards of It’s giant crystal ship can ward the monster away. There’s also a predictable but nasty plot twist involving Mitig’s true motives, which I won’t give away.

But the real draw is the live-action debut of a pretty important character from Stephen King’s mythos: Maturin. He appears to Neekani after she smokes some of Mitig’s herbs, and he informs her how her tribe can contain It for at least a few generations.

A character from both It and King’s The Dark Tower series, Maturin is a benevolent turtle-like deity powered by “The White.” His goodness, purity, and light stand in opposition to It’s darkness. He has a small but pivotal role in the novel, telepathically communicating with Bill and protecting the children during the Ritual of Chüd. He dies at some point after choking on a universe. Which kind of feels like a joke on the part of Stephen King, given that turtles don’t chew.

A Story of Derry is the quickest half hour you might spend this week. It’s a solid piece of American Indian horror, which remains a criminally rare occurance throughout mainstream pop culture. (The closest I can think of is 2022’s Prey, which is barely a horror flick, though A Story of Derry feels cut from the same cloth.) There are heavy allusions to the traumas of colonization, as well as the loss of land and way of life.

While Bill Skarsgärd doesn’t appear as Pennywise, sadly, “It” puts on a scary face as a creepy, pox-riddled Christian missionary who taunts Neekani’s mother. Still, like a bar of Twix at the bottom of a trick-or-treat pail, A Story of Derry is a most welcome surprise. Now we’re left wondering when season 2 will premiere. What’s the over/under on a Christmas surprise?

#6767. The 11 Best Fragrances Released This October

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The new smoky, spicy scents you need to know about.

I love fragrance. I love fall. Put the two together, and I’m in olfactory heaven. I’ve been excited to put this roundup together since the first new spooky scents started hitting shelves early last month—as we get into November, it’s evident that October will be a tough one to follow up.

There’s plenty of spice and smoke in the air, plus rich gourmands that feel tailor-made for colder weather. There’s even a new fragrance collection in partnership with Robert Eggers’s latest gothic horror film, for anyone who’s ever wanted to smell like they could turn into a werewolf at any moment—or, well, just want to smell like they’ve been at a bonfire. Ready to find your next fall scent? Read on for 11 exciting new fragrances you can get now.

If you’re looking for a new go-to fragrance for fall and winter, let it be Commodity Spice. Like a hot cup of chai, this expressive fragrance is warm and smooth with a rich cocktail of spices including saffron, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, and cinnamon. If I close my eyes, I feel like I just stepped into a cozy little tea and spices shop, and I want to wear that feeling like a sweater.

When Fulton & Roark released Cathedral of Ruins, it quickly became one of our favorite cold-weather smoky scents. Not only does it have a super unique aroma of smoldering frankincense, black pepper, rose, and woods, but it has a heartbreakingly beautiful origin story—the brand’s founders were inspired to create the scent after visiting the abandoned City Methodist Church in Gary, Indiana. The fragrance is an homage to the religious rituals that once took place in that church.

Think of a buttery croissant; a butterscotch candy; a cinnamon roll with sweet, creamy frosting. Those are the vibes of Gap’s newest fragrance. A late addition to the newly (re)launched collection of EDPs, it joins the group as the first gourmand—just in time for fall. Oh, and if you like how Bliss smells, you can complete the collection with the scented hand cream and body lotion.

I was always under the impression that fruity fragrances and woody ones had very little to do with each other and that, for the most part, they should stay separate. That’s until I smelled Maison d’Etto’s Pinehurst. Here, fruity notes of rambutan, blood orange, and ripe pineapple provide a beautiful overlay to base notes of leather, oud, and other woods. It’s a radiant scent that works year-round, day and night.

David Moltz (the “D.S.” of D.S. & Durga) was inspired to create this Resurrected Corpse Flower fragrance after visiting the Brooklyn Botanical Garden during the height of a rare blooming of a corpse flower. What he smelled was, in his words, “like a baby diaper pail in a rotten fish tank full of rubber lily bulbs & olives.” But then he got to thinking, what if that scent could be cleaned of all its rotten odors and reborn into something beautiful? Thus, Resurrected Corpse Flower was born. With green olive, lily, tuberose, freesia, and deep bog cedar, it’s a truly special scent that’s at once floral and swampy.

Because this fragrance is so unlike anything I’ve ever smelled before, it might be a bit polarizing; I’m sure some of you will love it, and others might prefer one of D.S. & Durga’s other unique fragrances. But after leaving this scent on my skin for a bit, I really started to appreciate it.

In contrast to some of the deep, rich gourmands on this list, Lumira’s Soléor offers a lighter, sun-soaked gourmand option. Instead of creamy sweetness, it’s more of a soft, sensual sweetness that isn’t too heavy or overpowering. Smooth amber and candied fruit up top give it a bit of a citrusy kick, which fades into caramel, vanilla, and woods. It works for fall and winter just as well as it does for spring and summer.

If you do want something rich and creamy, Phlur’s Heavy Cream is the way to go. It’s an ambery gourmand with notes of vanilla mousse, white orchid, and creamy musk, which are balanced out by hints of sparkling lemon and orange flower, adding a little bit of lightness to the otherwise heavy fragrance. And, of course, with a name like Heavy Cream, there has to be a coordinating whipped body butter for the full experience.

How do you make decadence refined? You create a rich, vanilla gourmand and add the sophisticated warmth of Peru balsam. It’s definitely a sweet scent, and the combination of Cristal vanilla, bourbon vanilla, tonka bean, and black sugar creates the aroma of a classic crème brûlée. But once you get past the creamy sweetness of it all, you’re left with a sensual, balsamic scent that lingers.

I didn’t know a fragrance could smell so much like Halloween, but Heretic teamed up with Robert Eggers’ new movie Werwulf and did just that. At first, you get spice and smoke from cardamom, smoke, and leather; it then moves into something woody, earthy, and animalic with fir balsam, labdanum, patchouli, moss, and damp earth. The “suggestion of wet fur” is what really makes this scent stand out—and what gives it that spooky edge. Wear with your scariest Halloween costume.

In a departure from the mostly spicy, rich, gourmand scents that hit shelves this October, Drake’s Better World Fragrance House partnered with October’s Very Own for a fresh, citrusy fragrance that gives the impression of a refreshing white wine sangria with notes of passion fruit, rose, white cedarwood, and roasted tonka bean. But in its spherical burgundy glass bottle, it’ll blend in perfectly with your other fall and winter scents.

Roll-on fragrance oils are all the rage right now, and new fragrance house Gamine has already come out with its own collection of fragrance oils called Microdose. With six parfum oils, you can wear each individually or combine two or three for your own unique scent. My favorite of the bunch is DMT, a metallic fragrance built on notes of burnt latex, aerated foam, and hot steel. I wasn’t sure I would like it based on the description—and the fact that I’d never heard of a metallic scent before—but I’m actually obsessed with it.

#6756. Skyler Gisondo on His New Fashion Campaign—and Dressing Like Harrison Ford in the ’90s

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The Primetime star is gearing up in Bonobos and getting ready for a very big 2027.

Skyler Gisondo is remarkably easy to talk to. If you’ve seen him on one of your various screens—whether as Decoy Dan from Primetime, Jimmy Olsen from Superman, or maybe just that meme of him from a decade-old red-carpet photo—you probably assumed as much. It’s the big smile, the friendly eyes, the freckles, the general sense of wholesomeness. But I can confirm it, because even though I know we’ve got a relatively brief window of time to discuss his new campaign with men’s fashion brand Bonobos over Zoom, we spend the first few minutes of our chat just … shooting the shit. It feels like catching up with a buddy you haven’t seen in a while. Relaxed. Natural.

Thankfully, the vibe continues as we start digging into matters of style. Gisondo tells me he’s always been interested in dressing well but hasn’t always known where to start. “I would see a cool dude walking down the street or something, and think, ‘Man, I want to look like that guy.’ But I never knew how. I always felt lost,” he says. He describes his 20s as a decade of “desperately trying on shoes that didn’t fit or something.”

He turned 30 recently, though, and “I really feel like over the last couple of years, I’ve homed in on my sense of style, what I feel good and confident in.” A very good time, then, to star in a fashion campaign—especially considering this seems like a breakout moment for the actor. He’s been working consistently since he was a kid, but his performance in Primetime as a young actor who gradually realizes just how toxic the entertainment industry can be has clearly launched him to another level. And he still has his upcoming role in Focker-in-Law this November and a couple more appearances as Jimmy Olsen (in Man of Tomorrow on the big screen and The People v. Gorilla Grodd on television) on the docket for 2027.

Over the course of our conversation, we touch on everything from dressing like a cowboy (a mistake) to using Harrison Ford in the ’90s as your style North Star (a very good idea). We also chat about the stuff he’s stolen from sets for his own wardrobe, the psychological validation of joining the Shrek franchise, and why, after Primetime, we can expect more creative big swings in the future. Read on for a few highlights.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

“It’s ultimately about your own confidence. I feel like the sweet spot for fashion is when what you look like reflects how you feel inside—when you get to this equilibrium and it allows you to be a more fully realized version of yourself. We all grow and our sense of fashion evolves with us but ultimately like I feel like there should be some current that runs through all of it. The stuff I’m drawn to is the more timeless, classic stuff. I look at Harrison Ford in the ’90s and I’m just like, it doesn’t get cooler, you know?”

“For a while, for whatever reason, me and every actor I know were like trying to look like a cowboy. And it just hit me one day: ‘None of us have ever worked a day in our lives on a cattle ranch, man.’ I don’t even know how to use a hammer! Like, what are we doing? Can we just be ourselves?”

“I’m pretty active. I surf and hike a lot when I’m at home. And I love walking; if I have an hour or two between meetings, I’ll just walk a few miles and take calls. I want something comfortable and functional, and I find a lot of vintage workwear just hits that and fits me well. And the story is so compelling to me. The idea of ‘Who’s worn this? What were they getting up to?’ ”

“What drew me to the campaign and to the clothes is that there’s a kind of timelessness to that style. My mom thought I looked amazing in the photos. My girlfriend too. My grandma and my sisters thought I looked great. It’s this very accessible and sort of classically cool thing they have going on. And I felt like me. I felt confident—so much so that I stole several items from the set.”

“With shows and movies, the fear is that it’s a one-of-one item that you might need back for another season. But that’s when you hit them with the ‘pretty, pretty please?’ You say, ‘I swear to God, I’ll guard it with my life.’ And they say, ‘Okay, but you can’t tell anybody.’ With a campaign, it’s probably easier because they’re excited for you to have it and represent. But probably 80 percent of my closet is basically just clothes stolen from characters and sets. It’s fun because you get to try on a bunch of versions of yourself and learn what you like.

“For instance, with Jimmy Olsen in the first Superman movie, they did a fantastic job with this retro-future thing. And then in The People v. Gorilla Grodd, they went a little more vintage-y in a way that felt more like me, Skyler, personally. I tried to steal almost the entire closet.”

“Well, right now I’m doing press for Primetime and Focker-in-Law. I’m doing another movie for A24 called Goblin that I’m not sure how much I can say about; I really don’t want to get fired. But I’m so excited. It’s the most insane script I think I have ever read, and it’s definitely a big swing. We have Man of Tomorrow coming out in the summer, and then Shrek 5. The number of texts I got when I got Shrek … ‘You made it, man! Oh my God! I had no idea you made it!’ I was like, ‘Thank you. Yeah, baby! Shrek 5!’

“But ultimately, it’s a very exciting moment because it’s the first time I have people asking, ‘What do you want to do?’ And I’m like, ‘Damn! I never really thought about that!’ I feel like Primetime lit a fire under me in a real way. And even though I’ve kind of been doing this my whole life, I feel a sense of drive that I’ve never felt really in this way before. So, yeah, man, I’m excited.”

#6755. Kendall Jenner Recreated a Cult-Favorite ’80s Movie Look for Halloween

With a November 3 birthday, Kendall Jenner started the celebrations early. The model threw a party on October 30 to fête Halloween and turning 31.

On October 31, she shared photos of her costume. The model transformed into Jane Henderson, the character played by Nastassja Kinski in Wim Wenders’s 1984 film Paris, Texas. The model traded her signature brunette hair for a chin-length platinum-blonde bob. She paired the look with a fuzzy, low-back hot pink minidress and sheer black tights. In one photo, she channels a memorable scene from the film, posing at a bar.

For those unfamiliar with the reference, Paris, Texas follows Travis Henderson, a mysterious drifter who reappears after four years away and attempts to reconnect with his young son and estranged wife, Jane. Directed by Wenders and written by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Sam Shepard, the film is considered one of the German filmmaker’s most celebrated works. It took home the Palme d’Or at the 1984 Cannes Film Festival and has since earned cult film status. More than four decades later, its imagery remains recognizable to cinephiles and fashion fans alike.

Jenner wasn’t alone in her cinematic costume. Actor Jacob Elordi joined her as Travis Henderson, the character portrayed by Harry Dean Stanton in the film.

While it marks the rumored couple’s first costume together, it’s not the first year Jenner has thrown a birthday party during Halloween weekend. In 2019, she teased that she was “keeping the Halloween birthday party alive for mom” on Instagram.

This year’s bash, which was thrown at Bar Marmont in Los Angeles, had a star-studded guest list. Attendees included Charli XCX, Hailey Bieber, Laura Harrier, and more.

#6752. Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet

For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format.

Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes.

Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

#6749. Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake

Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days.

Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine.

Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes.

Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed.

Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly).

Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes.

Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely.

Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6745. Taylor Swift Shows Why the Leather Pencil Skirt Is a Fall Staple With Her Latest Look

Taylor Swift is giving us another reason to revisit a classic wardrobe staple. The singer stepped out in New York to attend a screening of Toy Story 5 on November 1.

Swift showed up in an all-black ensemble, including a fitted three-quarter-sleeve top, pointed-toe pumps, and a leather pencil skirt that fell around the knee. With its combination of soft, streamlined tailoring and the slightly edgier texture, the outfit was a simple, polished ensemble.

Swift’s choice of skirt taps into the continued appeal of leather separates this season. While shorter leather styles have long been a fall favorite, the pencil silhouette is not to be forgotten, with its longer hemline lending itself particularly well to sleek, everyday dressing that can be dressed up or down. Kate Moss recently offered her own take on the leather midi skirt, further demonstrating the versatility of the piece.

Swift joined Toy Story 5’s director, Andrew Stanton, for a Q&A.

The singer contributed an original song, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” to the Pixar film, which was inspired by the story of Jessie, the cowgirl doll voiced by Joan Cusack.

In a clip, Swift shared why she connects with the storyline of Bonnie Anderson and Blaze Manoukian’s characters in the film. She recalled meeting her friend Abigail in Nashville when she was 14, who showed her the importance of “finding someone who is the same genre of weird and silly as you are.”

Their friendship has endured, with shared quirks like their love of doing Napoleon Dynamite impressions keeping them close. “It’s something our husbands have to put up with,” she said.

“When you find that person that completely sees you for the strange little genre that is you at your purest,” Swift reflected, “that hit me so hard watching the film.”

Kate completed the challenge back in June to raise funds for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, and revisited the milestone to thank the local mountain rescue teams “for the vital role they play in keeping walkers and climbers safe on the mountains all year round.”

#6743. Why Is It So Hard to Call Someone Out on the Group Chat?

Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

The screenshot, circulated in reporting on the allegation of sexual assault by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell in 2024, is painful to look at, and painfully familiar: a more extreme example of an episode that plays out on our own phones. Someone in the group chat says something fucked-up. You cringe as laughing emojis roll in. You think about saying something. You probably don’t. And you feel worse for it. Northwestern sociologist Aaron Shaw, who has studied how groups talk to each other online, explains why it happens.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

This kind of interaction is seen linked to the general disinhibition effects documented in digital communications: If your face isn’t there, and if you’re not confronted with the presence of other people, it’s a lot easier to behave in ways that may break with normal social conventions. There’s a long legacy of misogynistic groups existing and thriving. Some people might want to say, “Oh, this is a problem because of Snapchat,” but what research in the last 30 years suggests is that people will find ways to connect no matter what digital communication platform they are using. Research about online communities dates back to the 1980s and ’90s, and some of the high-drama incidents occurring in that time were around rape culture.

Gaming is an incredibly heterogeneous space of human activity, but there are some communities where violations of social norms are not just okay, but important: “If you want to play the game, you’ve got to get over it.”

They might be communicating at multiple levels in ways that are hard to see from the outside. By drawing on particular words they’ve used in the past, they might be signaling things to each other, like their membership in the group, their commitment to each other. Their desire to stay connected with each other may be more powerful than the desire to speak in an empathetic way about, in this case, the experience of a young woman.

Some research on bystander effects suggests that the larger the group size, the less likely any one individual in that group is to speak out against it. Individuals may feel like they don’t have control or that they can’t be responsible for the behavior of everybody in the chat. If their sense is that others in the group think this is okay—or would be willing to ostracize them if they were to speak out—they’re less likely to be willing or able to speak out.

There’s also a performative element. They are putting on a show; they are onstage for each other. Group chats really do serve that purpose. It’s hard to know what elements of that performance are, in a sense, fiction and what elements are a factual representation of the events that night in the frat house. The tropes these young guys may be using may be profoundly objectionable, may be hyper-misogynistic, may undermine the humanity and rights and autonomy of women, but it doesn’t necessarily equate to evidence of rape. In some ways it’s like cultural expression.

It might feel comforting to say, “Well, we can’t fix culture easily, but what we can do is kick people out of group chats or ban fraternities from campus.” But there’s lots of reasons to believe that that’s not going to actually address the root causes. There’s evidence that a lot of young men feel left behind or excluded by prevailing cultural and political and economic forces. I’m not saying that’s factually true, but the feeling seems to have made some young men hateful towards those they perceive to be not like them, who they perceive to be threats to their authority. It’s heartbreaking, not just for the alleged victim of sexual assault, but also for the people who engage in the chat. I don’t think that’s going to give them the sense of security and self that might allow them to behave more generously and respectfully towards others, either. ◼︎

Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

#6739. Chickpea Saag

This take-out staple is easy enough to recreate at home and fantastic for family dinners. If you’re looking for a comforting vegetarian weeknight meal, this stripped-down version is the ticket—it takes little time to prep, is both budget- and pantry-friendly (thanks to frozen spinach and canned chickpeas), and always goes down a treat. If you have kasuri methi or dried fenugreek leaves, crumble a healthy pinch into the spinach when you’re blending the mixture. It’ll make the saag even more fragrant and delicious. Leftover saag, if any, tastes even better the next day.

Find more delicious vegetarian dinner ideas here: Gochujang-Butter-Braised Tofu; Crispy Tofu With Peanut Sauce; and Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms.

Melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium skillet with a lid over medium heat. Add 1 large white onion, thinly sliced, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, coarsely chopped, 2 tsp. cumin seeds, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and tender, 8–10 minutes.

Uncover pan and add ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ½ tsp. ground turmeric. Cook, stirring often, until yogurt is slightly thickened (it will split into tiny curds), about 2 minutes. Let cool a few minutes, then transfer to a blender; reserve skillet.

Add ½–1 serrano chile (depending on the spiciness of your chile and your heat preference), one 10-oz. package frozen spinach, thawed, and ½ tsp. garam masala to blender; blend until mixture is very smooth, about 3 minutes.

Return purée to reserved skillet and add one 15-oz. can chickpeas, rinsed. Cook saag over medium-low heat, stirring often, until heated through (do not bring to a simmer or saag may split).

Transfer saag to a medium bowl. Serve with steamed rice and/or warm naan, lime wedges, and more yogurt alongside.

Do Ahead: Saag can be made 1 day ahead. Let cool. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Reheat over medium-low heat before serving.

#6737. Young Men of Cornell Want to Talk. Why Are Older Men So Quiet?

Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

One night in early October, activists broke a glass door at the entrance of Cornell University’s Day Hall, an administrative building that houses the office of president Michael Kotlikoff. They also vandalized its façade with the messages “Smash the patriarchy” and “At Cornell rapists are protected, protesters are expelled.” The next day, thousands of students and faculty gathered in Cornell’s Ho Plaza. When I stood in front of Day Hall, 36 hours later, much of the evidence had been erased. College life seemed to carry on as normal. Midterms, or “prelims,” were underway; students zoomed stoically past on electric scooters. The shattered panels had been replaced with planks and a sign directing visitors to an alternate entrance, and the graffiti had been power-washed to dark-gray smudges.

Cornell is situated among the gorges of Ithaca, New York, and I drove up from New York City to understand how men were making sense of a civil suit brought in September by an anonymous accuser, called Jane Doe in legal documents and media reports, alleging that she was plied with ketamine and sexually assaulted by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. All the men have denied wrongdoing. Jane Doe’s suit also alleges that Cornell failed to appropriately safeguard her from sexual assault. University administrators acknowledged that they had “fallen short and [are] taking meaningful action.”

According to punishment summaries obtained by The New York Times, Cornell had conducted a Title IX investigation, which resulted in the expulsion of two fraternity brothers and suspension of two others. The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office declined to pursue criminal charges. (New York governor Kathy Hochul criticized the Cornell police and the Tompkins County DA for their handling of the allegations and appointed attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate.) Among the materials included in Jane Doe’s suit was a photograph of a phone displaying a Chi Phi group chat, with reportedly more than 50 people, in which one of the men advertised Jane Doe’s “free pussy.” Some cheered. One asked if “the shop” was still open. In the screenshot, not a single voice raised an objection.

Men’s perspectives have been underreported during past sexual assault crises, perhaps out of the well-intentioned belief that we should prioritize listening to women. But when such moments to object to a woman’s dehumanization arrive, I wanted to know, why do men so often stay quiet?

Several people told me that my trip coincided with Ithaca’s most beautiful season, and, in person, the landscape did indeed look quintessentially autumnal. (My visit also coincided with the time of year in 2024 that Jane Doe alleges her assault in the Chi Phi house took place.) In the Arts Quad, Oscar, 21, was on his way to class, although he didn’t seem to have anything with him besides his phone. He was dressed in sweats and a boxy yellow tee, and he told me that he had joined a fraternity because he wanted to make friends. He had just left a Sexual Assault Prevention and Safety Club meeting for members of sororities and fraternities, where he and other students had discussed how the Greek system can develop stronger guardrails. One promising approach, he told me, was to delegate prominent members of frats to speak up about sexual assault. “It’s a scary and really hard conversation to have with your friend, especially somebody you think wouldn’t do something like that,” he said. “That’s what our meeting is about: How can we try to make these conversations more normal, more open?” Oscar was generous with his thoughts but grew reserved on the topic of fraternity culture.

Over by the Library or “Libe” Slope, an idyllic stretch of lawn on a rolling hillside, two guys tossed a Frisbee. I sat on the bench next to theirs while they hydrated. “A lot of people are saying, ‘If you were in that group chat, you should have said something,’ which I agree with,” said Hudson Tumey, who graduated last year. “You absolutely should have.” Tumey is a member of Cru, a Christian ministry on campus, and was visiting with William Canlis, a sophomore, who is also involved in Cru. “If I was in that group chat, I would’ve hoped with all my might that I would’ve said something,” Tumey said. “But I think I’d be lying to say that I would’ve for sure said something.” Tumey and Canlis explained that their faith offers them a man to emulate in Jesus Christ. “If a man doesn’t have that standard to look up to, that’s where bad things happen,” Canlis said. “If you don’t have Him, then what role model is left? The world? Look how broken the world is.”

I started looking around for other male role models. Near Sage Chapel, a non-sectarian church on campus, two clergymen visiting the campus said they hadn’t known about the Chi Phi case until that morning. One of them told me he preferred to stay out of it. Just outside Schoellkopf Field, an associate basketball coach asked me to email him. At the ROTC offices in Barton Hall, an Army poster read “Sexual assault. Sexual harassment. Not in our army.” A master sergeant paused his lunch to talk with me. He sat for a moment, then left to call his superior. After five minutes he returned and, with a half-apologetic inhale, said that he couldn’t speak with me until it’s brought up the chain of command and that I should email him. A roving police officer said that the only person on the force approved to speak with the press was Eric Stickel, Cornell University Police Department’s recently appointed chief of police, and I should email him. Ultimately, I approached almost two dozen non-student men associated with the town or the school and only one talked to me on the record.

At the Morrison Dining Hall, a seven-hour sit-in was underway, roughly matching the length of time Jane Doe spent in the Chi Phi house until she lost consciousness, according to the lawsuit. One of the sit-in’s appointed press contacts was John Hartnett, a 19-year-old sophomore representing Students for a Democratic Cornell, a group that had also helped organize the protest earlier in the week. He was proud of that turnout, as it was one of the largest protests at Cornell since the Vietnam War, but incensed by the irony of the school’s history of suspending students involved in other protests. He was also taking inventory of how he and his peers influence each other.

“It’s a difficult thing because you have to realize that some of your past actions—not sexual assault—perpetuated these things,” he said. “It’s something that men have to ask themselves: What am I not doing in terms of not holding the people around me accountable?” My phone rang. Someone from Cornell’s media-relations team informed me that the school was aware of my presence on campus and that none of the administrators were available for comment.

Reporters from Telemundo, The Ithaca Voice, and Reuters descended on Hartnett, and the sheer number of us bombarding him cast the reticence I encountered from his elders in a new light. While an inevitable chorus rose up to defend fraternities or disparage Jane Doe, some young men on campus seemed to be earnestly reckoning with the case or struggling to find their voice. But their community leaders appeared, at most, disconcerted. Perhaps those older men were grappling internally or opting for silent solidarity; whatever their reasons, I was struck by the persistence of their absence.

Later in the evening, I attended a Common Council meeting downtown at Ithaca City Hall. More than 50 people squeezed into a room set up for half that number. Ithaca mayor Robert G. Cantelmo oversaw the proceedings. A dozen or so students found spots on the floor; the local television station was filming. There were complaints regarding the closure of a parking garage, concerns about winter snow plowing, and, eventually, a proposed moratorium on some of Cornell’s event and noise permits, which was put forth as an effort to limit Greek-life activities. The floor was then opened for public comment, but only to those who had filed a slip.

“I think sacrificing some of the fun is more than justified by protecting people from these heinous crimes until the university gets off its rear,” John King, an Ithaca resident, said in support of the moratorium. “I applaud the city government for being willing to do so instead.” Sam Poole was a freshman when Jane Doe first reported her assault to the Cornell police. “I live in a Cornell co-op,” he said. “Co-ops host parties just like fraternities do, plenty of student organizations do, but we decided we’re not going to host parties until the moratorium is over.” Almost a week after the meeting, Cornell banned frat parties for the current academic year.

A few rows behind me, a man in a C-SPAN hoodie and tech pants was growing agitated that he had not been called on. “Michael Tracey,” he called out repeatedly. Mayor Cantelmo explained that Tracey’s name was not among the comment slips given to him by the clerk. “Motion to reconsider,” Tracey yelled out. “You’re definitely not eligible to make motions, because you’re not a member of this body,” Cantelmo replied. Tracey alleged his slip was thrown in the trash. “You should be ashamed for using the power of your office to conclusorily [sic] declare that any American citizen has committed crimes as heinous as gang rape before any semblance of adjudicative process,” he said as he walked out. I passed him my number.

Tracey asked to meet in the lobby of the Canopy Hotel. On my way there I learned that he is a contrarian Substack journalist, known for social media provocation; recently he argued that aspects of the Jeffrey Epstein case were overblown. He’s made multiple trips to Ithaca, where he’s filmed himself cross-examining students and faculty and showing up to public gatherings. He told me that he had driven from Jersey City to Ithaca to report on the Cornell case, motivated by his belief that Jane Doe’s identity should be made public. The previous week, he tweeted out her name before deleting the post. Internet sleuths published her address online. Then, according to Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, on the night before the meeting at City Hall, Jane Doe was swatted—that is, someone made a call to the police reporting invented violence at her home, prompting a large-scale police response. Giuffra told CNN that his client has been “terrified.”

Plaintiff anonymity is “used to manipulate the court system and thereby the public as a PR tactic to create pressure,” Tracey told me. “I have nothing against Jane Doe. She seems kind of cool, actually.” He showed me a text he sent to a number he claims belongs to her: “Given that settlement funds are being sought, especially considering that criminal investigations have been triggered, I consider it in the public interest to report on your identity.” When I pointed out that anonymity enables sexual assault victims to come forward with less fear of vitriol and death threats, he described the death threats he has received. This is what one of the loudest male voices I encountered in Ithaca sounds like.

I walked down Ithaca Commons to peer into Moonies, the bar Jane Doe visited before the alleged assault, but it was closed for the night. On Instagram, it appeared to be business as usual, with promotions for “Flash Friday” and “Saturday Surge” parties. In the suit, Jane Doe says she left a sorority event at this bar, went to another bar, and then “stumbled alone” to a party at the Chi Phi house. (Moonies is named in Jane Doe’s suit and its owners have denied that it illegally served alcohol to the underage Jane Doe.) I got into my car and headed to the frat. Even from the cozy confines of my rented Toyota Corolla, that path seemed uninviting. There’s a brick-and-stone charm to downtown Ithaca that dissolves once you cross over the gorges and onto frat row. Flashy trucks and clusters of mega-mansions run by very young adults bordered the drive. I spotted a handful of bongs resting on windowsills. For a minute, I couldn’t find the actual Chi Phi house and when I finally spotted it—massive, menacing—I was nearly relieved.

The next morning, campus cleared out for fall break. Visiting faculty member Mark Brown Jr. sat on the steps of Goldwin Smith Hall and finished a game of virtual chess before speaking with me. “I think frat culture is incredibly toxic,” he said. Some undergraduates in his art classes preferred to discuss the subject in a “roundabout” way. The potential of repercussions, he said, may be deterring open discussion.

I approached two students sitting under a statue of Andrew Dickson White, Cornell’s first president. “All men are honestly guilty for this,” said Daniel Suh, a junior studying public policy. “You ask any man if rape is okay and they’re going to tell you no. But men expect a perfect victim.” His friend, Anand Patel, also a junior, sat next to him. With their baggy pants and gleaming sneakers, Patel and Suh seemed so sweetly boyish, young, and on the brink of adulthood. But also fed up. While Suh felt regulating frat parties wouldn’t directly address the issue of college sexual assault, Patel was much more critical of frat culture. “Where the true issue lies is what happens when you have a friend who does it, or someone you know. Are you going to act like nothing happened? Are you going to support him, or are you going to cut him off? Because that’s ultimately what happens in these frats,” Patel said. “These men don’t draw a line in the sand saying, ‘Okay, you’re out now.’ ”

These students offered a stark contrast with the many older men I had tried to speak to, on and off campus, who couldn’t or wouldn’t add their voices to the conversation. For Patel and the other students I spoke to on campus, things seemed so clear: We should all call out bad behavior when we see it, because we know what bad behavior looks like. When did that get so complicated? ◼︎

Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

A sociologist who studies online groups explains how social dynamics play out on our screens.

#6735. Why Taylor Swift Hasn’t Been Seen at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs-Broncos Game in Denver

Taylor Swift has attended all of Travis Kelce’s home games this year, but during the Kansas City Chiefs’ away game against the Denver Broncos today, the singer wasn’t seen at Empower Field.

Swift was out earlier in the day in New York City, where she participated in a Q&A during a Toy Story 5 screening. She wrote the film’s song “I Knew It, I Knew You,” which has Oscar buzz.

Swift hasn’t been spotted at any of Kelce’s away games for the past two seasons, with security risks reportedly factoring into the decision. The tight end has a home game next Sunday, though, so she could be out in full force to support him and his teammates then as they face off against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium.

While she has regularly attended Kelce’s games throughout their three-year relationship, Swift has never deliberately drawn attention to her appearances. As she told Time in December 2023, “I’m just there to support Travis. I have no awareness of if I’m being shown too much and pissing off a few dads, Brads, and Chads.”

“I don’t know how they know what suite I’m in,” she added. “There’s a camera, like, a half-mile away, and you don’t know where it is, and you have no idea when the camera is putting you in the broadcast, so I don’t know if I’m being shown 17 times or once.”

Last year, Swift attended some of Kelce’s games without being photographed. Over the course of her career, she has mastered the art of entering and leaving places undetected. In an October 2025 interview with Scott Mills on BBC Radio 2, she revealed that this would be her greatest asset as a spy.

“Just put me in a garbage can, roll me, I don’t care,” she said. “Honestly, I can fit in like, a purse. Sometimes I just can’t deal with it [the paparazzi and attention] and in those times, I won’t deal with it. I’m just digging tunnels under every building I go into, airlifting in through the skylight.”

#6732. Are Frats Just Gangs by Another Name?

This article contains descriptions of allegations of sexual assault. Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

I grew up in Amherst, Massachusetts, 10 minutes from frat row, a strip of filthy, dilapidated mansions long since demolished and bought by UMass. When I was a child, I went trick-or-treating there and received rolls of toilet paper for my trouble. Then, as a teenager, I went there because it seemed like a place where nobody would stop me from drinking, or otherwise try to protect me from anything. It was a kind of slumming, an escape to a decrepit environment mostly beyond the reach of the law. The first time I hung out with people who drank themselves sick, it was at a frat party. My first rock show and mosh pit too. Driving around town, my friends and I chauffeured hitchhiking frat boys from one party to another. The town was full of people who liked to criticize rich people, but frat boys and other students actually threw stuff at rich people. As a longstanding winter tradition, UMass students marched onto the campus of small, elite Amherst College, pelting students with snowballs, but also, reportedly one year with rocks, obliging Amherst College’s president, the following year, to threaten to call in the state police. But to me, their apparent lawlessness made them exciting, the local equivalent of Vikings.

Later, I wrote a book of short stories about frat boys, interviewing many of them in the course of my research. So when news spread that a woman had filed a civil lawsuit alleging a horrifying gang rape had taken place at the Cornell chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024, people asked me how such a thing might have happened.

Much of the Cornell affair is shocking. But it’s especially repugnant that the young men in question, who have denied wrongdoing, apparently wanted to have sex with a woman who was, according to the plaintiff’s account, so far gone on alcohol and ketamine that she could barely be considered conscious. “I was a sex doll for all intents and purposes,” Jane Doe told a police interviewer, according to reporting by The New York Times. Her intoxication, according to the lawsuit, was extreme. Indeed, it could have been a kind of coping strategy: “My thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out,” she’s reported to have told officials. And what was happening inside the minds of the men? The suit includes a photograph of a Snapchat group, where one of the brothers texted other active members to “pu” (“pull up”) for “free pussy.” What could make a man advertise an intoxicated woman’s body for the apparent purposes of sharing her with his male friends?

Since Jane Doe’s civil lawsuit was filed, much has been written about hazing rituals in general, which some pundits argue socialize members to be violent toward pledges, and women. But there is also a blend of homophobia and homoeroticism that has a long history in American fraternities. The anthropologist Peggy Reeves Sanday, in her 1990 book Fraternity Gang Rape, related the account from a woman who lived in a frat house for a summer and described a “circle dance” that took place, invariably, to the Doors’ song “L.A. Woman”:

The song comes on and the brothers start yelling “Ho! Ho! Ho!” All the brothers link arms and join in a circle. Then the whole circle moves around so fast that the shortest members are lifted off the ground. The “Ho!”s continue until the circle loses control and the entire group piles on top of each other, squashing the smallest members […] For a bunch of guys who were always so full of nasty, ugly, homophobic remarks, they seemed to enjoy jumping around on top of each other very much.

In some cases, there have been homosexuality-detection rituals in fraternities that are not only implicitly anti-gay but deeply homoerotic. Pledges, according to one of the accounts in Sanday’s book, were told to expose their genitals, with actives (an “active” is an active member, that is, a full-fledged brother of the fraternity) punishing those who refused with push-ups. Other rituals are just plain homoerotic: Pledges might be asked to simulate sexual acts in front of others, or forced to shower together, or consume liquor through the anus.

There’s a history, too, of frat boys using women as accessories for homoerotic revelry. In 2015, the Indiana University chapter of the Alpha Tau Omega fraternity had its charter revoked after a leaked video showed a crowd of actives watching as one of their brothers, prone on a mattress and stripped to his boxers and socks, looks to be performing cunnilingus on a woman, who, the chapter’s chief executive officer said, was a hired exotic dancer, and whose legs seem to keep him in a headlock. Some men sit on the floor nearly naked, watching passively, while others stand over him fully clothed, spanking their brother or patting his back. It’s unclear to what degree, if any, the frat boy giving oral sex is being coerced, but it seems clear from his state of undress that he’s been cast as an object of desire. The woman appears to restrain him, forcing his face into her crotch. She is there, it seems, to perform dominance for both the amusement and the titillation of the frat.

The horrors alleged at Cornell seem to have taken place in that space between amusement and titillation. One of the Chi Phi’s on the now infamous Snapchat included in the lawsuit about the alleged gang rape sent a text about how a brother “went in 7 min ago and is not afk” (“away from keyboard”). Another, one of the men in the purported original threesome with Jane Doe, added something seemingly like an exhortation: “Like you can walk in and whip it out.” If word had gotten around Chi Phi that a threesome had taken place between two of the brothers and Jane Doe at the proposition of one of the men, as is alleged to have happened, they might well have been ridiculed or, worse, made to feel like outsiders. Their brothers might have asked, Who did what with whom? Did they like it? Some of their brothers, in other words, might have made a supposition about their sexuality.

It’s possible to interpret the Snapchat messages as an effort to turn a MMF threesome—with its potential suggestion of male bisexuality—into something more heterosexual. According to Jane Doe’s lawsuit, one of the two Chi Phi’s “forced oral sex on Plaintiff” while the other one “slapped Plaintiff on the buttocks multiple times, resulting in bruising.” According to the claims in the lawsuit, this might have been the beginning of a long slide into the alleged drug-fueled violence—Jane Doe treated as a shared resource, like a pizza or a keg.

According to Thomas Giuffra, Jane Doe’s lawyer, she learned of the Snapchat exchange thanks to a picture taken by a fraternity member not present. A few days after the alleged assault, she saw other users condemning Chi Phi on an online forum, as detailed in text messages accessed by The New York Times.

“Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?”

“They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore. Report them.”

Those posts reportedly started to shift Jane Doe’s perspective about what had happened to her. “That’s the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted,” she reportedly told investigators. The posts laid bare a chilling facet of Greek life: A fraternity that discards its proclaimed values (“Chivalrous behavior crosses the ages to touch the heart of Chi Phi,” reads the creed of the frat) can start to look like a middle-class gang.

In a foreword to Fraternity Gang Rape, longtime Philadelphia trial judge Lois G. Forer remarked on the similarities between frat boys and urban street gang members, having tried both in her courtroom. Fraternities and gangs, she said, both “engage in sexual behavior that others call gang rape,” considering it “a form of male bonding for which the female is merely an available instrument.”

But there is another similarity that Forer neglected to mention: a fraternity, like a street gang, can derive much of its power by controlling access to an illicit resource. A street gang might control access to cocaine or heroin in a particular neighborhood; a fraternity, at a university located in a small city like Ithaca or Amherst, can act as the gatekeepers to a large, conveniently located house in which there might be little to no supervision or check on the consumption of drugs and alcohol. That is what brought me, as a curious teenager, to frat row, where underage drinking and other mischief appeared to be abundant.

According to text messages published by CBS, about a week after allegedly being raped at the Chi Phi house, and a couple of days after seeing the “Crips or Bloods” comments online, Jane Doe seemed to consider attending Chi Phi’s upcoming Halloween party.

“Chi phi is your house and you are welcome here,” a frat brother wrote, reassuringly. “Thank u i really appreciate that,” she replied. “<3 i’ll bring my cigs tomorrow.”

Soon after, though, she reportedly said she received a call from the chapter president disinviting her from the party. The dismay and anger she expressed in response—“yall aren’t my friends” and “the woman will always get the short end of the stick”—seem to be a testament to how central Chi Phi’s parties were to her social world, to Chi Phi’s outsize power to ostracize in the insular eddy of the American college campus.

Those within a fraternity fear ostracization, too, and they might take dramatic measures to avoid it. In Sanday’s book, she describes a brother “so worried about his attractiveness and masculinity that he set quotas for sexual encounters for certain time periods.” Sex was not merely about pleasure, “but the feeling of acceptance and approval” it might generate. The alleged violence at Cornell smacks of these anxieties, the need to transform sexual intercourse into a performance of masculinity. A healthy fraternity, committed to the cultivation of young men, might allay these anxieties rather than exacerbate them. The frat would be a place to practice alternative forms of masculinity, inculcated by a house where vice had no foothold. But then, would anyone go to their parties? Would the fraternity even survive?

As a high school kid, I wanted to live within a fraternity’s nimbus of approval. Instead, I lived with my mother, most of the time, and it was she who had taught me how to shave. I didn’t play any sports, wasn’t on a team or in a club. I was drawn to fraternities, then, for some of the same reasons boys in poor neighborhoods are drawn to gangs: loneliness, boredom, the need for male role models.

One autumn night, not long after rush week, I walked by one of the frat houses and witnessed a spectacle unfolding on a lawn: pledges, arrayed single-file, dressed for a day at the office, in sweater vests, ties, oxford shirts, khakis, and brogues. An active, pacing the line like a drill sergeant assessing the combat readiness of new recruits, barked about the importance of neat tie-knots and aftershave, of steaming your pants and polishing your shoes. The pledges listened in silence, rapt with attention, their ties crooked, their sweater vests ill-fitting, their bearing less than military, some of them fidgeting, and shifting their weight from foot to foot. They would have done anything their pledgemaster said, so total was his air of authority and their need for it. I would have too—believing, in my innocence, that he could have taught me how to be a man. ◼︎

A fraternity at UC Berkeley in the 2000s.

In 2018’s The American Fraternity, artist Andrew Moisey presented intimate photographs of Greek life at his alma mater (see above) to reveal the paradox of fraternities: Pledges take oaths to help each other become ideal men, then revel in behaving badly. Now a professor of art history and visual studies at Cornell, Moisey tells GQ: “It feels [like] we are in an abusive relationship with the fraternities. They tell the task forces that they’ll never do it again, but they’re built on breaking their own promises. If the fraternity is helping Cornell’s graduates go on to high places, then, I guess, isn’t that good for Cornell? But when there’s a death [like that of Antonio Tsialas, whose body was found at the bottom of a gorge two days after an unauthorized Cornell fraternity party in 2019] or an alleged rape or any other kind of tragedy, our association means that what they do dishonors all of us.” For Moisey, the debate now playing out among faculty, administrators, trustees, and donors about the future of frats at Cornell boils down to an “old, classic” question: “What’s more important, honor or money? Cornell is supposed to represent enlightenment. Does this look like enlightenment to you?”

What people in Ithaca are saying—and not saying—about the sexual assault allegations brought against members of the Chi Phi fraternity.
