#6713. The Best Men's Crewneck Sweatshirt in 2026, According to GQ

There’s no such thing as ‘the best men’s crewneck sweatshirt,’ at least not in the objective sense. As tactile and quantifiable garments can be, the truth is it’s all open to interpretation, and comes down to personal taste (even if your personal taste sucks). That said… I do have some strong opinions on what makes a good sweatshirt and have tested too many to name. I grew up wearing cheap, serviceable sweats from places like Walmart. I’ve also invested in unreasonably heavy 24-ounce sweatshirts and became obsessed with the unyielding craftsmanship of Japanese reproductions that required rare loopwheel machines.

Through decades of experience, I’ve honed in on what makes a sweatshirt special. A good crewneck sweatshirt should be comfortable, and that all comes down to fabric and fit. The fabric, usually made of either a French terry or a brushed fleece, should be both dense and soft. The silhouette shouldn’t squeeze, but should be relaxed enough to layer over a T-shirt or even a button-up. I’ve also dialed-in on the things you should avoid, like when sweatshirts are too tight in the neck, especially as a guy with a thicker gullet for my frame. And I really hate when sweatshirts are too long. As a long-torso individual, you’d think this wouldn’t be a problem, but it’s something that feels endemic to the genre.

Now that I’ve given you a brief tour of the weeds, let’s get into what you came here for. Through rigorous research and far too much time on our hands, here’s what’s what in the world of crewneck sweatshirts.

Reigning Champ has been in the sweats game for generations, producing some of the absolute finest hoodies, sweatpants, and crewnecks around. When I was first introduced to the brand an unspeakable number of years ago, it left an impression on me. The idea that something so basic could be so good revealed to me that my base line for quality was much lower than I’d realized.

Though we here at GQ have adored their slim-fit crewnecks for years, Reigning Champ's more classic-fitting sweatshirt is one that will stay steady through the fickle fashion trend cycle. It's made with custom-knit midweight French Terry fabric, cut with a relaxed but clean fit, and sewn with super smooth flatlock seams to cut down on bulk. While most sweatshirts will opt for either raglan sleeves or set-in sleeves, Reigning Champ’s crewneck stands out for its unique construction that uses both techniques. The result is a more tailored set-in sleeve look at the front with raglan details at the back to give the wearer a freer range of motion.

The brand’s name alone sets high expectations, and in every aspect, Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt meets and exceeds them. While $125 isn’t by any means cheap, the stunning quality from the fabric to the fit and finish all equate to a sweatshirt that punches well above its weight class. If I really had to nit-pick, though, I'd like to see the color palette expand a little more, especially for such an essential piece of kit.

If your sweatshirt budget is decidedly smaller, your first stop should be Russell Athletic, the Alabama sportswear stalwarts who literally invented the crewneck sweatshirt way back in 1926. Almost a century later, they're still turning out the best bang-for-your-buck fleece crew on the market. It's got all the classic details that made Russell a household name: ribbing at the cuffs and hem, a V-insert collar, and a classic cut (size down if relaxed ain't exactly your thing).

The midweight 9 oz. fleece is pleasantly soft and warm, and it's moisture-wicking and breathable so if you run a little hot, it won't emphasize the sweat in ‘sweatshirt’. The thing I like most about Russell’s crewnecks is that they still fit like the vintage joints—but you don’t have to work yourself to death bobbing between vintage stores trying to hunt one down.

No list of the best crewneck sweatshirts would be complete without Champion's reverse weave joint in the mix. Todd Snyder’s legendary collab (see below) has got style and function down pat for the new-school, but the OG heavyweight pullover deserves a crown of its own. The sturdy cotton-poly blend is soft but will hold its shape after countless wash cycles (loungewear and pizza go hand in hand—residual stains do not). Fabric aside, the fit is just right: not too slim, not too baggy, and with slightly dropped shoulders to make your neckline really pop. We pick quality over quantity any day, but with this classic sweatshirt you get the go-to year-round layering piece for the fewest amount of dollar bills.

If you’re expecting a soft, motherly embrace, I hate to tell you this, but Champion’s iconic Reverse Weave sweats aren’t the softest. In fact, they’ve got a pretty rough hand. But don’t worry about that too much because that’s just straight out of the box. What you get in return is an unquestionably beastly durability. And the longevity you get out of them means they’ll only get softer and luscious with age.

You can’t ignore the impact that vintage clothing has on the modern fashion landscape, not just for the endless references and inspiration it gives designers, but also for the sheer explosion of secondhand style. Vintage-obsessed dudes like myself will search high and low for forgotten garments with esoteric details, from jeans left in abandoned barns to rare leather jackets tucked away in grandpa’s attic. And if you’re thrifting skills aren’t up to snuff or if coughing up the dough to a dealer is too big of a hit, the best thing to do is to look to Japan where they’re even more obsessed with reviving the grails of bygone eras.

While many repro brands deserve their flowers, I’m particularly keen on Buzz Rickson’s' interpretation of the perfect vintage sweatshirt. The fabric is made using ultra rare loopwheel knitting machines that knit the terry material methodically and slowly, using the natural tension of gravity to achieve a product that’s shockingly soft for its density. It also results in a fabric that’s totally seamless around the torso, an old-school detail that’s hard to come by but oh-so-satisfying once you do. The crewneck sweatshirt also features low-profile flatlock seams, tall ribbing at the cuffs and hems, and the throwback V-neck insert for easy donning.

HAVEN's Excel crewneck employs the label's telltale details like custom ribbing and underarm gussets for increased range of motion. But the star of the show has to be the fabric which comes from rare 1980s Azume knitting machines, lauded for producing low-tension French terry with unrivaled softness and character.

Lady White Co.'s methodical approach to jersey knits has brought them to the top of the heap not just for tees and sweatshirts, but for the entire wardrobe. It's mini crewneck uses custom-milled terry fabric that's cut to a flattering cropped silhouette and garment-dyed for depth.

Look, I'm just as surprised as you are that Gap's heavyweight sweatshirt is not only $70, but actually that good. It's legit heavy and will handily knock out other sweats in beefier weight classes, especially since you can often find it on a mega discount.

The kings and queens of American-made cotton fleece at Camber make their crewneck from a beefy 12-ounce cotton fleece with just enough elastic in the body panels to make it feel like a big hug. Plus you can get it in 11 colors.

Dyed one at a time by hand, each sweatshirt from the New York-based indie label Buckets is completely unique and certainly distinct from the droves of potassium-dyed, sun-faded, vintage-inspired sweats that have flooded the market in recent years.

NYC-based 3sixteen has built out a line of carefully dialed-in menswear, like this hardy crewneck made with a fleece that's, quote, "some of the heaviest available on the market." And yet it's the pockets, surreptitiously slipped into the side seams, that have us nodding in appreciation.

Known for its chef-approved T-shirts, Whitseville's reproduction sweats deserve equal praise for its heavy all-cotton fleece, tubular construction, and double-V gussets that reference rare vintage crewnecks.

Quince's 70-30 cotton-poly blend recalls vintage sweats of yesteryear, the kind that were as soft as they were durable and didn't break the bank. Its Everyday fleece crew ticks all the boxes.

There are levels to sweatshirts, as humble as they are. What we look for in high-quality sweatshirts comes down to fabric, construction, and fit. Sweatshirt fabrics should be soft, certainly, but many high-quality options are quite burly and stiffer than you'd think. Most of the time, that means the more material goes into the sweatshirt the longer it'll last. And if you're willing to commit to them, they'll get softer and more comfortable the more you wear and launder them.

Most garments are made by overlapping fabrics and sewing them together. That may be fine for a dress shirt, but sweatshirts are made of a thicker, knit fabric which can bulky and irritating when it's sewn like this. We like sweatshirts that are made with flatlock seams which are made by butting two fabrics next to each other rather than overlapping; the result is a smoother, flatter seam. On rarer occasions, some sweatshirts are made the old-school way on either tubular knitting machines or very rare loopwheel knitting machines which produces a sweatshirt without any side seams on the body. Garment nerds go gaga over this kind of detail, but it's by no means a requirement for a good sweatshirt.

Sweatshirt fabrics are typically made from terry cloth, French terry, or brushed terry. (If that sounds familiar, it's because terry cloth is the same stuff that's used to make bath towels.) Terry cloth features loops of yarns which are absorbent and insulating. But the main difference between your bath towel and your sweatshirt is that sweatshirts only have the loops on the inside of the garment. Often, those loops are either brushed or shorn to give the material a luxuriously fluffy hand.

Fit is always subjective, but classic-fitting sweatshirts will fit somewhat relaxed all-around and fall at the hips. Slimmer sweatshirts will fit better if you want to layer them under a jacket and look cleaner with slim-fitting pants. For a fit that's more of-the-moment, opt for a sweatshirt that's boxier and cropped to go with some high-waisted, baggy trousers.

The humble crewneck helped Steve McQueen evade capture in The Great Escape, cemented John Travolta’s heartthrob status in Grease, and made Eddie Murphy a badass in Beverly Hills Cop. Paul Newman, the patron saint of laid-back menswear, wore one religiously. And today, a roster of famous—and famously stylish—dudes still put their trust in it. The only difference now is that it comes in a rainbow of different colors and silhouettes, not to mention fabrics far beyond the staid French terry.

Like many menswear staples, crewneck sweatshirts were born from athletics and have transcended into everyday leisure. You could style a crewneck with baggy jeans and sick sneakers for a streetwear-leaning aesthetic, dive headfirst into a preppy look with a pair of chinos and loafers, or turn up the lounge-factor and double it up with some sweatpants and classic sneakers.

Like The Bachelor, we had a flock of hopefuls vying for our love. But instead of hot singles, we had to dole out roses to a gaggle of cozy sweatshirts. One by one, we got to know each sweatshirt, taking them out on dates (literally), and looking intently for rock-solid characteristics, flaws, and dealbreakers. We wore every sweatshirt like any other piece of clothing in our closets, styled them with our favorite pants, scrutinized their fits, put them through harsh laundry cycles, and repeated the whole process over again. What we ended up with is this A-team of great crewnecks, from budget options to luxurious upgrades, and everything between.

#6706. The Best Men's Jean Jacket 2026: 12 Fall Layering Essentials

Adding the best men's jean jacket to your closet is like drafting Lebron to your rec league team: you’ll end up with a ‘ship no matter how bad the rest of the squad is. Whatever you want to call ’em—jean jackets, denim jackets, trucker jackets—the all-American stalwarts are the layering MVPs of every outfit on the brink of an L. Makes sense considering blue jeans, the jacket’s southern equivalent, can do the exact same thing for your wardrobe. Workwear roots bestow the humble piece of outerwear with utilitarian features, durability, and classic proportions—a surefire formula that churns out menswear icons like double-knee pants and chore coats.

What started out as a work jacket to accompany the blue jeans made from the same burly denim material, jean jackets have grown out of their pragmatic uniform and are more of a fashion statement these days. Be it a luxurious runway riff, an upgraded take, or a down-home workhorse, every flavor of denim jacket has the potential to make every outfit pop. Of course, the trucker jacket is what comes to mind first. But denim jackets come in many forms and aren’t limited to the Levi’s version you likely have in your mind’s eye. Denim’s enduring appeal and boundless applications have seen it merge with chore coats, trenches, Harringtons and more, expanding the scope of jean jackets. That’s great news for anyone looking to find one that truly speaks to themselves, but terrible news for anyone attempting to wade through all the options.

So we did the denim digging for you. We went out and scraped the market for the absolute best men’s jean jacket, from the tried-and-true to the new-age startups and everything in-between.

This shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone. And if it is, as this company’s self-proclaimed Denim Guy, it’s definitely my fault for not teaching you. Levi's is the grand daddy of all jeans which puts them on a rarified level few others could ever hope to approach. The brand’s iconic 501 jean gets most of the (deserved) praise, but the Levi's trucker jacket also warrants recognition.

The very first iteration of the Levi's trucker jacket debuted in 1905 and has since gotten several updates, but the one most ubiquitous today is known as the Type III. It's the picture you have in your head when you think of a trucker jacket and it's great for so many reasons. The midweight denim is ideal for year-round wear, the trim and cropped silhouette has transcended trends for decades and, like the five-pocket blue jean, pairs with just about everything (and looks better the more you wear it). If you only have a hundred bucks to spare and enough room for just one denim jacket in your rotation, it had better be this one.

A chore coat isn’t what most people think of as a ‘jean jacket’. But I’m proposing this as a more practical, no-less stylish alternative to the usual trucker jackets you’re used to seeing. And if you’re taking the term ‘denim jacket’ liberally, any outerwear made of denim would count. Anyway. Chore coats are more commonly made of a sturdy canvas or heavy moleskin cotton fabric, but denim's resilience make it another reliable option for the workwear genre. It doesn't get much better than this one from Alex Mill.

The brand's range of modern menswear staples is no slouch when it comes to fabric and construction and its line of chore coats is among the best out there, even compared to the multi-generational stalwarts like Carhartt and Dickies. This one’s made with sturdy, yet broken-in 100% cotton Japanese denim and comes with dual chest pockets and hand pockets, not to mention a stealthy phone pocket. The relaxed fit borders on boxy and is roomy enough to layer over a sweater or thick hoody once the temps drop. But if you're not the denim type (why are you even here?) Alex Mill makes its work jacket in a range of different fabrics, too.

To me, Alex Mill’s chore coats are nearly perfect. They fit like a dream and come with just the right vintage details that make guys like me swoon. I’ve compared it with my vintage French chore coat and not only are the details almost identical, the craftsmanship is virtually the same. So you could search for hours for a vintage one, or you could save the time and money and just get Alex Mill’s.

Levi’s may be the dominant denim trucker jacket, but they aren’t the only ones with a classic trucker jacket etched into the annals of menswear history. Lee’s left an indelible mark on the American denim landscape and is rightfully considered one of the so-called Big Three along with Levi’s and Wrangler. Lee’s famed Rider jacket was first introduced in 1948 and is considered one of the best denim jackets of all time.

Today’s modern reproduction is made by the brand’s retro sub-label, Lee 101, and features the same left-hand twill denim the brand is famous for, this time woven by a storied Japanese denim mill. The signature zig-zag stitching details at the collar and front placket still remain, as do the cateye buttons at the waist, and the slim, hip-length silhouette. If you’re hardcore, I’d recommend you go with the raw denim version and earn those fades yourself. But if you can’t be bothered to put in the work for five years straight, then stick with the light wash version.

Fans of the Japanese brand Kapital are quick to point out the brand's head-spinning takes on denim. From painstaking boro patchwork stitched by hand to far-out interpretations of blue jeans, the cult-loved label is a true innovator in the denim space. Its catalog is chock full of certified grails, but if you’re focusing in on jackets, it doesn’t get any crazier than its boro jacket. From the outset, it looks more like an antique pile of fabric than a jacket—and that’s kind of the point. The jacket is made of dozens and dozens of fabric scraps, each one meticulously distressed—and then repaired— to look like worn-out vintage textiles before sewn back together as a single garment.

As you can imagine, the process is extraordinarily time-consuming. That immense dedication results in a jacket that’s truly not for the faint of heart or those with shallow pockets. This particular jacket takes inspiration from Type I denim jackets and features a single flap pocket, rear cinch, and a boxy cropped fit. It may look shredded, but putting it on feels like absolute butter thanks to the custom, boro-printed satin interior.

Kaptain Sunshine has long been known for its loving recreations of heritage American workwear, but the artful way it approaches its designs has earned it a ton of crossover appeal with the fashion crowd. Case in point: This one-pocket denim jacket, which is constructed according to classic selvedge standards, but has enough interesting details (including a buckle back) to inspire the envy of any runway show attendee. Wear it carefully—you never know which menswear nerd could be nearby and hoping to swipe it from your chair.

The circle of iconic denim jackets is small. Even so, there’s one that doesn’t get as much attention it ought, and that’s the Type II trucker jacket. Levi’s introduced the Type II in 1953, the long-awaited follow up to the Type I. The features were much the same, but the main difference was the addition of a symmetry-imposing second pocket and adjustable waist tabs instead of a cinch back. The result is one of the most geometrically pleasing jackets ever. The boxy fit and spare details are very much in line with workwear designs, but there’s something also very minimalist about it, too. No wonder it still gets referenced and duped by modern designers.

Levi’s will always be the OG when it comes to the Type II, but if you really want to get one, The Real McCoy’s is the one to get. The Japanese brand is known for going insane lengths to reproduce the most coveted and iconic pieces of vintage menswear and their rendition of the Type II is a prime example. The denim was designed from the ground up, using a specifically sourced vintage loom that was able to deliver the kind of slubby character of ‘50s denim at a consistent clip. The result is one of the most accurate reproductions you can get. That is, if you can even find it. Thanks to the limited fabric production and high demand, the jacket is so sought after that it’s been sold out for ages.

Don’t let Gap’s iconic khakis ads make you forget that the iconic brand got its start in denim. That DNA is still prevalent today as Gap’s stable of denim offerings is as strong as ever. Case in point, this faithful take on the famous Type II trucker jacket featuring knife pleats, dual chest flap pockets, and a boxy cropped fit—all done in a hearty all-cotton denim.

If we didn’t tell you, you might not realize this was denim too. But even though it's finished in soft corduroy, there's a full denim jacket inside, taking trompe l’oeil to a new level. While most attempts would easily fall flat in the uncanny valley, Jeanerica's result offers the best of both worlds (and textures).

Before Ralph launched his western-inflected RRL line, Polo was still making workwear hits. And denimheads could easily miss this pitch-perfect take on the Type II trucker jacket with its impeccable cut and spot-on vintage wash.

J.Crew and Lee's collaborative iteration on the denim jacket is a true sleeper hit, featuring a mix of details from a corduroy collar, trendy (and practical) plaid lining, and those beautiful, unmistakable Lee trucker pockets. This is the denim jacket to take with you into fall.

Ralph's premium ranch-hand line has been quietly making the best faded denim in America for decades: The 'Leeland' wash has genuine depth to it, and even better—the buttons are embossed with “Cowboy.”

Material and construction: With denim jackets and jean jackets, the most important factor will be the denim itself. Make sure that the denim feels substantial and weighty. Good quality denim shouldn’t be too thin or loosely woven. Though I personally prefer denim without any sort of elastane, you may want to consider opting for a jacket with some stretch built into it for ease of movement. Even then, I’d advise you to limit the percentage of stretch to no more than 2%. Selvedge denim and Japanese denim are often a good sign of a high-quality fabric, but non-selvedge and non-Japanese denim can be well-made too, so don’t put all your trust in provenance.

Fit: Fit is subjective, but most trucker jackets follow a tried-and-true formula with a hem that hits right at the hips. They may have a leaner silhouette or a boxier cut, but a hallmark of trucker jackets is truly the cropped length which helps emphasize your natural proportions and lengthens your legs (without having to spend tens of thousands of dollars and months of agony). Denim jackets with hand pockets are often a little longer than those without, so if you may want to factor that into your decision.

Silhouette: Sizing is key, as well. Most denim jackets are cut on the more tailored end and around hip length. Make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your shoulder bones if not a little past. Keep in mind that you may want to layer underneath, since that will affect how snug the jacket will feel. With time, the sleeves of a trucker jacket will tend to get shorter as the elbow creases set in so if the sleeves are a tad long, you’re probably in a good place.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6702. 33 Gifts for Wives Who Hope You've Been Listening

One of the great pleasures of being married is bearing witness to your life partner's tastes and obsessions. And you'd think all that inside knowledge would make buying her a gift a cinch, and yet here you are, looking up the best gifts for wives. No judgment—we've been there. Whether it's an anniversary, a birthday, or just an occasion to remind her how much you appreciate her, we've rounded up a few things that have been on our radar all year. And yes, you should probably make that dinner reservation, too.

Still got names on your list? We've got ideas. Peruse the rest of our gift guides, and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a regular dispatch of things we think are worth your money.

It's easy to get distracted by all the excellent cashmere at Banana, but the brand knows its way around silk, too. This shirt is cut roomy and relaxed, with the sort of effortless drape that makes getting dressed easy.

Coach's Empire Carryall comes in a whole family of sizes, all cut from the brand's soft glovetanned leather. It's a beautiful bag on its own, but I'd suggest picking out a few charms to dangle from the handles to make it hers.

Phoebe Philo's Peak sunglasses are aptly named: the shape is, quite simply, peak. An absolute stunner of a pair, and just imagine her walking into brunch wearing them.

Depending on whom you ask, the Moon Shoe might just be Nike's defining sneaker of the moment. Credit Jacquemus, whose collaboration turned a relic of the brand's running history into one of fashion's most coveted shoes.

J.Crew has barn jackets on the brain this year, and its considerable efforts might just have you lusting after one yourself. I'm partial to the studded version, but there's plenty to choose from, including corduroy and faux shearling renditions.

A silk scarf is an endlessly good gift, if only because there are endless ways to wear one. Around her neck, in her hair, knotted onto a handbag, however she pleases, really.

Brooches are all over the runways right now, and might just be the easiest way to lend an outfit a little extra panache. This dangly little number from Lie Studio features carnelian stone, with a rich, brownish-red hue that feels of the moment.

A coworker Chris first put me onto Simuero, but it wasn't until a trip to Barcelona earlier this year that I got to see the Spanish jewelry label's work in person, at Bassal Store. Beautiful stuff, with an organic, slightly imperfect quality that's even better up close.

This is about as chic as it gets, as far as under-eye patches go. The silky patches promise a little firming power, and the set also includes the Le Lift hand cream as an extra treat.

Makeup, of course, is a tricky thing to gift, but a colleague of mine showed up to the office wearing this purple blush from Violette_FR, and I was immediately sold on the shade. I've had it on my running list of recommendations ever since.

Soft Services has shrunk its beloved exfoliating Buffing Bar down to miniature proportions, with four little bars in a very giftable set. A posh way to keep skin in check, and low-key great for travel.

There was plenty of oohing and aahing when a small sample of Maison Francis Kurkdjian's Oud Velvet Mood landed on my desk this year. A gorgeous oud with notes of peach, suede, and leather.

Dr. Sturm has built quite a following for her science-minded approach to skincare. This travel-friendly set brings together some of her signature formulas, all tucked into a fuzzy fleece bag.

Sidia's Braless Duo pairs a subtly scented mist and serum, a welcome salve for winter-weary skin.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

One floral and bittersweet, the other peachy and citrus-forward, these botanical aperitivi are deliciously complex without trying to taste like booze. Serve over ice or topped with soda.

Caraway isn't the first to make a coffee maker with an all-glass-and-steel brewing system, keeping hot coffee away from plastic. But it might just be the best-looking of the bunch, which counts when it's one of the first things they see in the morning.

What, your dinner parties don't involve serving salad with horn-handled, mother-of-pearl spoons? Gohar's nautilus shell-inspired salad servers are spectacularly unnecessary, which is why they make such a great gift.

Hario might be best known for its coffee gear, but the Japanese brand knows its way around matcha, too. This gift set includes a double-walled glass bowl and everything she needs to prepare a prower bowl of matcha.

Just the thing to christen that new matcha set. Kettl sources its teas directly from growers, and I'm currently taken with its Okuju matcha. Developed with a longtime partner in Uji, Japan's storied tea-growing region just outside Kyoto, it's a particularly fine powder with a delicate nuttiness and a wonderfully smooth finish.

Edie Parker's gemstoned lighter case has long been a go-to gift around these parts, but this year we've got our eye on the matching ashtray. No smoking equired—it makes a pretty fab catchall for jewelry, keys, and other little things.

I love the freaky pop-art vibes of this collaboration between Dusen Dusen and Venetian glassmaker Laguna~B. The pitcher is great on its own, but you can also spring for the set with two matching glasses.

Apple's new AirPods 5 come in two tiers, and the more giftable of the two is the version with the wireless charging case. You get longer battery life and swipe-to-adjust volume controls right on the stems.

For the record collector, U-Turn's Orbit Plus is one of the finest midrange turntables around. This version has a built-in phono preamp, so she can get straight to spinning records with a pair of powered speakers.

Taking its cues from Kodak's '70s-era 110 camera, Camp Snap offers a screen-free digital experience with an 8MP sensor, which is modest by today's standards, but entirely the point.

Nothing says great gift quite like an overengineered personal fan she'd never buy herself. Dyson's bladeless design is the clever bit, delivering a steady stream of air that's whisper-quiet.

If she's going to track her health, she might as well do it with the latest Oura Ring. The fifth-gen model is 40% smaller, with more proactive insights and personalized guidance to help her make sense of all that data.

Electric toothbrushes aren't exactly paragons of sustainable design, but Suri is doing its damnedest to change that. Its Pro 2.0 has recyclable plant-based brush heads, a repairable body, and a rechargeable battery designed to keep the whole thing out of a landfill for longer.

How could Theragun possibly improve on its already excellent mini massage gun, you ask? By adding heat, of course. The Mini Plus combines percussive massage with warming therapy to help loosen up sore muscles.

If cupping is good enough for the sporting elite, it's certainly worth a spot in her recovery routine. Wthn's kit includes eight silicone cups for a gentler take on the practice that can still help relieve muscle tension.

Wonder Valley's hinoki-scented bath products have won over a few of GQ's more relaxation-minded staffers. This set pairs a handsome bar of soap with a sachet of bath tea, which can be steeped a few times before it's finally spent.

Red-light technology is coming for sex toys, and Lelo's Mona Spectra is among the first to get in on the action. Expect to see plenty more of it in the years ahead, but there's nothing wrong with being an early adopter in this particular department.

#6699. Dutch Apple Snacking Cake

Every autumn the siren song of baking calls bakers home until the volume becomes too much to bear. And at that moment, the only thing that can silence it is a warm-spiced apple cake—the kind that hugs you closer than a knit sweater. This recipe, which keeps things simple, relies on the winning combination of cinnamon and apples to perfume a vanilla cake with pockets of tender fruit. A blanket of cinnamon streusel crowns the cake, giving it a contrasting crunch and a coffee-cake-like character. Feel free to stash the cake on your counter, slicing it throughout the week, enjoying its plush interior as it magically gets better with time.

More cozy bakes this way: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Chocolate Olive Oil Cake; and Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly coat an 8x8" metal baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Lightly coat parchment with nonstick spray. Place 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (packed; 200 g) light brown sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, in a large bowl and mix with your hands, squeezing together as needed, until marble-size clumps form. Set streusel aside.

Toss 1 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 2 large), peeled, cored, thinly sliced, slices halved crosswise, and 2 Tbsp. (16 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to coat.

Whisk 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and remaining 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to combine. Add ½ cup (1 stick) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until no visible pieces remain. (Mixture should look like lightly moistened sand. Don’t worry about overworking it.) Add 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup buttermilk, 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract and stir until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Mix in about two thirds of apples.

Scrape batter into prepared pan and spread into an even layer; smooth surface. Scatter reserved streusel and remaining apples over, letting them organically intermix. Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 65–75 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan. Using parchment overhang, lift cake out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Dust with powdered sugar and cut into 12 pieces if serving immediately.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 5 days ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6696. 4 Epic New Watches Every Watch Guy Is Salivating Over Right Now

Welcome to Watch Guy Watches, GQ’s monthly curation of high-end timepieces for the true watch nerds among us. This month, Moser goes retro(grade); Lange brings back a beloved bracelet; Biver drops its first hand-wound three-hander; and Breitling puts a pair of vintage-inspired watches in its core catalog.

There are only a few firm absolutes in the horological sphere. One of them is “never bet against H. Moser & Cie.” The high-end independent maker never ceases to amaze with its creativity, wit, and technological prowess. From a mechanical timepiece that bears a suspicious resemblance to a certain famous smartwatch to one the coolest integrated bracelet-bearing luxury sports watches on the market, Moser consistently delivers the Swiss-made goods.

Building upon its Pioneer Retrograde Seconds Midnight Blue release from two years ago, three new models with retrograde seconds join the collection this month in the Pioneer, Endeavour, and Streamliner collections. While all three are beautiful, however, it’s the latter whose aesthetics pair particularly well with this steampunk-esque complication—one in which a small hand tracks the passing seconds in an arc and then jumps back to its starting position at the top of each 30-second period.

Housed in a 40mm brushed stainless steel cushion case with a serpentine integrated bracelet, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds offers a potent mix of Streamline Moderne and futurism before one even considers its dial. Executed in midnight blue fumé enamel, it features applied indices and the brand’s signature modified syringe handset, with a faint “H. Moser & Cie” signature appearing in white beneath 12 o’clock. The lower half of the face, meanwhile, is given over to the retrograde seconds display. Inspired by instrument gauges such as automotive speedometers, it features smooth action powered by the cal. HMC 252, a product of movement specialists Agenhor. (Flip the watch over and you can view its tungsten rotor whirring away via a sapphire caseback.)

One of the coolest features of the Streamliner collection is that despite the presence of numerous complications; of the use of fumé dials; and of high-end pricing, these watches are meant to be used. With 120m of water resistance, steel constriction, automatic winding, and 72 hours of power reserve, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds is effectively a high-end tool watch. (Though at a sticker price of 29,900 CHF, maybe take it off if you’re, like, climbing Mt. Everest or whatever?)

While retrograde seconds displays don’t have the same utility as calendar readouts or GMT complications, they do demonstrate horological competence on the part of the watchmaker…and more importantly, they’re wild fun to watch in action. And if you can’t have a little fun in your watch-collecting journey, well—then what the heck are you even doing here, anyway?!

If you’ve been waiting years for the return of platinum bracelet options for A. Lange & Söhne’s Datograph Perpetual watch, we give you permission to rejoice: a new version of the timepiece—made in honor of the model’s 20th anniversary—is equipped not only with a diamond-studded black dial, but with a fresh matching platinum bracelet. Designed with five links rather than the seven of early-2000s models made by German jewelry manufacturer Wellendorff, said bracelet is perhaps more notable than the watch itself, which features the brand’s manually wound manufacture Calibre L952.1 movement and is limited to just 50 pieces.

When watch-world elder statesman Jean-Cladue Biver and his son Pierre co-founded their eponymous firm in 2022, their introductory product was a half-million-dollar automatic tourbillon and minute repeater. Having since added a simple automatic three-hander to their lineup in the form of the Automatique, they’re now expanding their offerings with a hand-wound three-hander in stainless steel. Dubbed the AB, it measures 38mm wide and 9.8mm tall and features a beautiful black multi-level onyx dial with gold accents, plus a cool stainless steel bracelet with an angular five-link design and a patented micro-adjust system. Powered by the new Calibre JCB-004 designed in collaboration with Le Cercle des Horlogers, it’s the brand’s entry-level model…though it’ll still set you back roughly the cost of a BMW M3. (Naturally, it’s already sold out.)

On the slightly less eye-watering—but no less compelling—end of the watch-guy spectrum is the new Breitling Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41. Why does it look so familiar, you might ask? Effectively, it’s a modern version of the famed ref. 806 “Twin Jet”-logo chronograph from the 1960s, only this time, it’s available as a non-limited edition—a fact that will surely excite deep Breitling aficionados. Measuring 41mm in stainless steel, it’s manually wound just like its vintage namesake, and comes paired to a brown leather strap for $7,900 or to a handsome steel bracelet for $8,400. If you fancy something a bit more left-field, there’s also a hand-wound, non-limited version of the Cosmonaute, a riff on the Navitimer equipped with a 24-hour dial that was famously worn by astronaut Scott Carpenter in 1962 ($10,600-$11,000).

#6695. Zendaya Recreated an Iconic Halle Berry Fashion Moment for Halloween

Zendaya didn’t miss out on all the fun this Halloween. The actress dressed up as one of Hollywood’s most enduring screen and style icons, Halle Berry, thanks to a special vintage pull.

On Saturday, Zendaya’s longtime stylist, Law Roach, shared a series of photos of the Dune actress recreating a particularly memorable early-aughts look that Berry wore: a butter yellow, brown, and white printed string bikini top with silver accents and matching low-rise, wide-leg trousers from Lanvin’s fall 2000 collection. Zendaya completed the look with pointed-toe heels.

Roach thanked Lanvin’s artistic director Peter Copping and Alix Long in his post. Copping took the creative reins at the French fashion house in 2024, and Cristina Ortiz was Lanvin’s womenswear designer when the fall 2000 collection debuted.

Berry first wore the two-piece to the New York premiere of X-Men in July 2000. She accessorized with a belly chain and tinted sunglasses.

Berry saw the tribute and posted her approval on X. “She won,” Berry wrote of Zendaya.

The fashion homage feels particularly fitting given that Zendaya has been drawing comparisons to Berry since debuting her pixie cut.

In fact, when Zendaya first unveiled the look at the 2026 Emmy Awards in September, Roach confirmed that the haircut was inspired by Berry’s iconic short hairstyle.

Berry later embraced the tribute, sharing Roach’s interview on her Instagram Story and writing that Zendaya “murdered the night.”

This isn’t the first time Zendaya has used fashion to pay tribute to another star. In 2013, she channeled the late Aaliyah for Keep a Child Alive’s Dream Halloween, recreating the singer’s iconic Tommy Hilfiger campaign look. More recently, she honored Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in a vintage Bob Mackie design.

Zendaya and Roach have more fashion moments ahead: The actress’s Dune: Part Three press tour is just kicking off.

#6689. Everything You Need to Know About The CFDA Awards

Nominees and winners, celebrity attendees, and more

Tonight’s CFDAs are like the Oscars of American fashion. The biggest awards presentation of the year, the evening celebrates design talent and creativity here in New York and across the country. These honors are determined by the CFDA Fashion Awards Guild, an invitation-only voting body of industry peers—fashion editors and journalists, retail executives, stylists, influencers, and other industry professionals—many of whom will gather for the ceremony tonight at New York’s Museum of Natural History.

This year, highly anticipated categories include Womenswear Designer of the Year, whose nominees include both industry heavyweights like Michael Kors and younger talent like Diotima’s Rachel Scott. Google Shopping’s American Emerging Designer of the Year is also a hot category, with buzzy nominees like Emily Dawn Long, Colleen Allen, and Zane Li of Lii. There will also be a number of celebratory honorees, including Tory Burch, who will receive the Positive Change Award, and Anthony Vaccarello, departing creative director of Saint Laurent, who will be given the title International Designer of the Year.

The Council of Fashion Designers of America has guaranteed a star-studded event. Alongside host Keke Palmer, presenters include Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, Naomi Osaka, Cole Escola, Demi Moore, and Cornelia Guest.

To brief you on all the necessary information ahead of the announcements, we’ve aggregated the nominees, awards, and relevant details surrounding them—and will be updating the list with the winners in real time.

This year’s roster of nominated designers spans generations of American design talent, and each has had a significant role in shaping what women’s fashion looks like today. Every nominee is returning. Khaite’s Catherine Holstein has won twice, in 2022 and 2023; Rachel Scott, now head of Proenza Schouler, won for Diotima in 2024; and Michael Kors won in 1999. (He’s also received a number of other honors, including the Lifetime Achievement Award, from the CFDA.) Tory Burch and Wes Gordon of Carolina Herrera have each been nominated in this category once before.

Based on the year he’s had, Zane Li of Lii is the front-runner in this category, which was won last year by Ashlynn Park of Ashlyn. So far in 2026, he has won the CFDA Fashion Fund and the Fashion Trust U.S. Ready-to-Wear Award; he was also a runner-up for the LVMH Prize. But he has competition: Julian Louie of the artistic label Aubero and Colleen Allen of the buzzy, Victorian-inspired eponymous brand were both nominated in the category last year and have each been named LVMH Prize finalists in recent years. Newcomers include Julia Ferentinos of Juju Vera, who has shot to prominence for her antique-inspired jewelry beloved by fashion It girls, and Emily Dawn Long, whose crochet hats and viral slogan tees made her a favorite among both the downtown set and the Instagram algorithm.

The menswear nominees are all familiar to this space. Ralph Lauren has won CFDA Awards in both menswear and womenswear, alongside the lifetime achievement recognition. Mexican American designer Willy Chavarria is also a returning winner; he received this award in 2023 and 2024. Thom Browne took it home for the fourth time in 2025. Public School won in 2014. Snyder has never won but has received multiple nominations.

The accessories category presents an interesting mix of nominees. The Olsen twins have won this award numerous times for the beloved bags and shoes from the Row. Raul Lopez of Luar has won twice, and he’s coming off a year of launching a buzzy handbag collab with MCM. Stuart Vevers won in 2017, and his affordable leather goods for Coach continue to capture shoppers’ attention across generations. As for the final two on the list—both modern minimalist jewelry designers—Ana Khouri has received multiple nominations in this category, while this is Sophie Buhai’s first nomination.

The Positive Change Award goes to Tory Burch.

The Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award goes to photographers Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin, typically referred to as Inez and Vinoodh.

The International Designer of the Year Award goes to Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, who exited the label this fall after a decade at its helm.

The Media Award in honor of Eugenia Sheppard goes to Eva Chen, vice president of fashion at Meta.

The Founder’s Award in honor of Eleanor Lambert goes to Linda Fargo, as the SVP fashion and store presentation director is celebrating three decades at Bergdorf Goodman.

The Isabel Toledo Board of Directors’ Tribute will be presented to Susan Cianciolo, for her RUN collection.

#6686. Samira Nasr’s November Editor’s Letter: On Performance

From Natalie Portman to the dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White, this month’s issue is all about those whose art takes place in front of an audience

I’m writing this from Paris as the Spring 2027 shows are wrapping up. One glorious night, I had the chance to see Céline Dion during her residency at the Plénitude Arena. What really struck me about her performance was her unique ability to unite an entire stadium. It was just her up there—no background dancers—using her voice to bring us along on her journey. It was deeply moving. I was reminded of how vital performance can be. I’m sure there were people in the arena whose lives and experiences and politics differ from my own, but we could all come together to revel in the sheer joy of an incredible show.

That is the spirit in which we celebrate this issue’s theme, performance. A performer can entertain us, transport us, and, crucially, connect us.

Our cover star, Natalie Portman, photographed by Carlijn Jacobs and styled by our style director at large, Malina Joseph Gilchrist, has consistently transported us over the years with great performances. In the coming months, she will deliver two more, in Cathy Yan’s biting art-world satire, The Gallerist, and in Lena Dunham’s hyped new rom-com, Good Sex. Both reveal a lighter, more humorous, though by no means less committed side of Portman, and that’s by design. “Right now,” she tells our executive editor, Leah Chernikoff, she’s focusing on “a lot of joy. I think it’s both for myself and what I hope to offer an audience. There’s a lot of really heavy stuff going on … and so it does feel like the biggest service you can do right now as an artist is to deliver some joy.”

Elsewhere in this issue, I am thrilled to feature a range of dancers, musicians, writers, and actors whose work I have long revered. The dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White came together in conversation to discuss their new stage adaptation of the classic American novel and film Imitation of Life, which also marks Legend’s first musical. “At the core, this is a story about the American dream, with all of its contradictions and complications,” says Nottage.

Sarah Hoover brings us the story of one of ballet’s great modern partnerships—American Ballet Theatre’s Isabella Boylston and James Whiteside—as they prepare to dance their final performances together. Boylston, who welcomed her first child this summer, returned to the barre six weeks after giving birth in order to be ready to partner with Whiteside before he retires next summer. “If I had to go onstage with him tonight in Swan Lake, with zero rehearsal, I’d still feel good about it,” Boylston tells Hoover.

When this issue is on newsstands, our podcast, The Good Buy, cohosted by Chernikoff and our executive digital director, Lynette Nylander, will be back for its fourth season, available wherever you get your podcasts and on YouTube, featuring another incredible lineup of folks whose style we’re obsessed with, including Paloma Elsesser and Kim Kardashian. Each episode is a reminder that getting dressed is the ultimate performance.

Opening image: Celine cape and dress. Tiffany & Co. Bird on a Rock by Tiffany Wings earrings.

#6682. 7 Celebrity Outfits You Should Steal This Month

With the holidays looming and next year’s awards season on the horizon, there’s no rest for the A-list weary. Between hitting up screenings, press junkets, and the general business of being a star, you’ll occasionally catch famous folks kicking their feet up in suites at SoFi Stadium or risking a courtside collision with a referee at an NBA game.

From Harry Styles getting his heart rate up on morning runs over the Williamsburg Bridge to Ethan Hawke turning up for a SAG screening, Glenn Close pulling an absolute grail piece from a film she starred in alongside Robert Redford, and Nicholas Hoult hopping between planes, the celebrity style circuit is showing no signs of slowing down.

Maybe this is the season you’ve been influenced to go all in on corduroy, resurrect those vintage graphic tees gathering dust in your tote bins, or finally dip your dainty toes into the jazz shoe craze. Whatever your sartorial itch, let these celebrities do the legwork for you.

The Hawkester has worn corduroy before, and this look calls to mind Robin Williams in Dead Poets Society, whose affinity for the fabric felt like part of the curriculum. Hawke styles the suit in a way that feels less adjunct professor and more stoner student, thanks to a ratty graphic tee and tinted shades. Rather than dress shoes, he opts for well-worn dark brown Sambas, which contrast nicely with his acorn-colored suit. Carpe diem, and all that.

The star of Netflix’s upcoming show The Altruists demonstrates how dressing in a flowy, monochromatic palette doesn’t have to feel boring. The burgundy trench coat injects just enough color to keep things interesting. Leave it open so you don’t look like Inspector Gadget, and throw on tinted sunglasses, because they’re never a bad idea, no matter the fit.

With his Together, Together tour wrapping up at the end of the month, Harry’s New York stroll fits will likely be inducted into the annals of celeb big fits. He seems to have tapped into the lore of ’90s-era skaters, layering a long-sleeved tee under a T-shirt. Add light-wash jeans, all-white sneakers, and Apple earbuds, and you’ve got a man who feels gloriously analog in a digital world.

Glenn Close shows us how to build an outfit around a statement piece, in this case, a jacket from The Natural, the 1984 film in which she co-starred. Throw on navy slacks, loafers, and a crisp white Oxford shirt, and you’re good to go. Of course, it helps when you have iconic films attached to your name, too.

Example 1,088 of why denim-on-denim is always the answer to the in-flight outfit dilemma. Mr. Hoult opts for a charcoal-hued Canadian tuxedo, offset by black boots and a dad cap. Denim can take a beating. Whether from turbulence-induced coffee spills or an overenthusiastic recline, it provides a welcome layer of warmth on those cold and bone-dry flights.

As the oldest brother in Sweden’s Skarsgård acting dynasty, Alexander proves that an age-old graphic tee and Chuck Taylors will always be a can’t-miss combination. The louche, open trench coat adds a bit of flare to the fit. We also have to note, when you’re 6’4” with a chin chiseled enough to double as an ice luge, it’s hard for anything to look bad on you.

People love to claim that black and brown don’t belong together. I guess they’ve never had a Turtle Pecan Blizzard. The black shirt and blazer flirt with Y2K corporate-core, but the khaki-colored, pleated, baggy chinos and jazz shoes give the whole kit some much-needed attitude.

#6673. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Adding cottage cheese to a meatball might sound like an attempt to cram extra protein into a recipe, but it’s not the only valid reason. Something magical happens with the addition of cottage cheese: It practically disappears in the baking process, lending the meatballs juiciness and a subtle savory-salty flavor. As a bonus, the cottage cheese helps to stretch the recipe and you’ll end up with almost twice as many meatballs from one pound of ground beef.

Think of this recipe as a bit of a blank canvas, allowing you to use the meatballs however you please. You can bake them and pop them in your mouth as is, drop them into simmering tomato sauce, or stuff them between slices of bread for a hearty sandwich. They, like most meatballs, are also very meal-prep-friendly and take to freezing well.

More great cottage cheese recipes this way: Cottage Cheese Lasagna; Cottage Cheese Caramelized Onion Dip; and Roasted Honeynut Squash With Cottage Cheese and Chili Crisp.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Mix together 1 large egg, 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, one 16-oz. container cottage cheese, 1 lb. ground beef, 1 cup Italian breadcrumbs, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large bowl to combine. Scoop out into 2-Tbsp. (heaping) portions and roll into smooth balls between your hands (you should have about 30).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large nonstick skillet over high heat. Working in batches and adding more oil between batches as needed, cook meatballs in a single layer, turning halfway through, until browned on 2 sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet and bake in oven until cooked through, 12–14 minutes.

Do Ahead: Meatballs can be made 3 days ahead. Let cool; transfer to an airtight container and chill, or freeze up to 1 month.

#6671. Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?

At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”

I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

#6668. Salt Bread (Shio Pan)

Welcome to the Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep into why it works. This month we welcome deputy food editor Hana Asbrink to be our guest baker. Come bake and learn with us—and don’t forget to join the Bake Club group chat over on Substack.

The version of this recipe that appeared in our November 2026 print issue has the incorrect bake time listed. The recipe that follows features the correct total bake times of 15–18 minutes (please see step 8).

Salt bread is a wondrous buttery roll known as shio pan in Japanese or sogeum ppang in Korean. It originated in Japan in 2014 and quickly became popularized in Korea soon thereafter, taking off in the post-Covid era around 2021. It’s formed by rolling each ball of dough around a nub of salted butter. As it bakes, the butter melts and oozes out of the bun, “frying” and crisping up the bottom. If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer.

You’ll often find a range of salt bread, some leaning closer to sturdy bread with a tighter crumb and others resembling a softer milk bread. In all salt bread cases, there are a few key identifiers: (1) a deeply golden exterior, with the aforementioned crisp bottom; (2) the signature hollow in the middle (where the pat of butter once stood) when you tear the bun in half; and (3) a sprinkle of flaky or coarse salt atop the bun.

In this riff, I use an enriched dough, bringing in qualities of a soft milk bread into the mix. With the bread flour, the end result is a lovely, crowd-pleasing bun that’s great for snacking on its own or enjoying alongside a special holiday meal. If there’s one note to highlight: Ensure you are starting with a fresh pack of instant (or “rapid-rise”) yeast. This will make all the difference in the rise and the eventual yield.

Read More: BA Bake Club’s October Recipe Is the Best Dinner Roll We’ve Ever Made

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 3 hours 30 minutes for resting)

Stir 2 Tbsp. (16 g) flour and ½ cup water in a small skillet, preferably nonstick, over medium heat with a heatproof rubber spatula to combine and cook, stirring constantly, until thickened to the texture of mayonnaise, about 2 minutes; remove from heat. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into small pieces and stir until melted. Transfer tangzhong to the bowl of a stand mixer.

Add 2 large eggs, ½ cup whole milk, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) to tangzhong; stir vigorously by hand with rubber spatula until incorporated. Add remaining 4 cups (500 g) flour, attach bowl to stand mixer fitted with a dough hook or paddle, and mix on low speed until dough is smooth and soft (it may stick to bottom of bowl but should mostly clear sides), 20–25 minutes. Pinch off a small piece of dough and stretch it between your thumbs and index fingers on both hands. The dough should be able to stretch thin enough to let light through without breaking. If it tears, the gluten is not yet developed enough. Keep mixing until it can stretch; it may take up to 30 minutes.

Transfer dough to a work surface (no need to flour) and shape into a ball. Lightly grease stand mixer bowl with vegetable oil. Return dough to bowl, cover tightly with a plate or plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm, draft-free spot until nearly doubled in size, about 2 hours. (For optimal flavor, let dough sit at room temperature 30 minutes, then cover tightly or transfer to an airtight container and chill at least 8 hours and up to 2 days to proof slowly.)

Meanwhile, cut 1 cup (2 sticks) salted butter into 1-Tbsp. pieces and arrange in a single layer on a large plate or small baking sheet. Chill in freezer until ready to use.

Transfer dough to a surface (no need to bring to room temperature before shaping if you chilled it). Using a bench scraper or paring knife, cut dough into 70–75 g portions (you’ll get 12–16 portions depending on how much your dough has risen). Working with 1 portion at a time, cup your hand over dough and drag across surface, moving your hand in a rapid circular motion to form into a tight ball (cold dough is easier to work with; rolling into balls on an unfloured, ungreased counter creates friction and helps the shaping process). Place on a baking sheet and cover with plastic wrap; let sit 15 minutes.

Uncover dough (save plastic wrap) and, working one at a time, carefully roll each ball into a cone shape with your hands (you want them about 4" on the wider end). Return to baking sheet and re-cover with reserved plastic wrap. Let dough rest 15 minutes.

Place a cone in front of you on surface with wider end facing toward you (keep remaining cones covered in plastic wrap). Lightly flatten with your palm, then roll out dough lengthwise to make an isosceles triangle about 12" long with a 3½"–4"-wide base (short side of triangle). Place 1 Tbsp. frozen salted butter at base of dough and roll up (not too tightly) like a croissant. Arrange, seam side down, back on baking sheet. Repeat with remaining cones and salted butter (you may not need all of the butter; save it for another use). Let rolls sit at room temperature until slightly puffed, about 1 hour.

Place a rack in lowest position in oven; preheat to 425°. Remove plastic from rolls. Lightly mist rolls with water from spray bottle; sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake 10 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back and continue baking rolls until golden brown on top and bottom, 5–8 minutes more (keep an eye that they don’t burn). Remove from oven (there will be melted butter on baking sheet, so be careful) and, using a heatproof pastry brush, brush butter on baking sheet over rolls. Let rolls cool at least 10 minutes before serving.

Do Ahead: Rolls can be baked 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6667. Better American Sunscreens Are Here—But We’re Still Way Behind the Best

Anyone who’s applied sunscreen only to be left with a chalky white cast, a greasy finish knows American sun care has long been a frustrating experience. The US is decades behind European and Asian counterparts, which have long been blessed with sunscreens that are lighter, more luxurious, and easier to wear every day. For skincare obsessives (this writer included) trips abroad are also opportunities to stock up on superior sunscreens they can’t find at home.

The root of the problem is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration classifies sunscreen as a drug rather than a cosmetic. Because of that distinction, more time and testing is required to get new sunscreens on the shelves, dramatically reducing innovation in American sun protection. But for the first time since the ‘90s, we’ve had some movement on that front. In June of this year, the FDA approved a new sunscreen filter called bemotrizinol—also known as Tinosorb S or BEMT—after years of lobbying in the states by dermatologists, skincare brands, and Congress members. It’s a meaningful step toward better sun care, but the US is still lagging behind.

Bemotrizinol is prized for its ability to provide both UVA and UVB protection while remaining stable in sunlight. That’s a significant advantage over some existing US-approved filters, which offer protection against one type of UV radiation more effectively than the other. BEMT also has the potential to make sunscreen more pleasant to wear: “And because it’s a large, oil-loving molecule, it mostly stays on the surface of your skin instead of soaking in, and it blends into lightweight, non-greasy formulas with no white cast,” says Dr. Joel Spitz, co-founder, chief medical officer, and board-certified dermatologist at Honeydew, a virtual dermatology platform.

Bemotrizinol might be new for the US market, but it’s already been used in sunscreen formulations abroad for 20 years, Spitz says. That long track record helps explain why consumers in the US have spent years coveting the more cosmetically elegant formulas available in countries like South Korea and France. While most consumers would love if major brands like Neutrogena, La Roche-Posay, or Beauty of Joseon brought their European or Asian formulations to the US, those SPFs still contain filters that the FDA hasn’t approved. As a result, many brands are developing entirely new BEMT-centric formulas for use stateside.

Australian label Ultra Violette was the first brand to release a BEMT sunscreen in the US with its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in August 2026. Neutrogena debuted its Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 in September. Earlier this month French drugstore staple La Roche-Posay put its Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 up for sale online. Don’t mistake the relatively quick arrival of these products after the FDA’s approval for ease in which brands can develop new formulations. According to Emanuella Louis, La Roche-Posay’s public relations manager, the brand had been working on its new formula for more than two years.

That long lead time reflects the way sunscreen development works: Brands can research and test formulas in anticipation of regulatory changes, then move a product forward when a particular filter gets the green light. Louis says La Roche-Posay has access to filters the FDA may be considering for approval and is “actively working, playing, testing on what possibly those formulas would be.” When a filter is approved, she explains, a formula already in the testing pipeline can be moved up.

Some brands are still tinkering with BEMT formulas for the US. Round Lab, one of South Korea’s most popular sunscreen manufacturers, has sold a version of its SPF in the US since 2024, and is hard at work on a new version of those formulas that contains bemotrizinol.

“Bemotrizinol’s approval in the US is a meaningful change, but it does not mean a Korean formula can simply be brought to the US market as is,” says Koochul Kwon, Round Lab’s chief technology officer. Beyond incorporating the newly approved filter, brands must ensure the ingredients keep the UV filters stably dissolved and working alongside other components, including moisturizing ingredients. The finished product must then meet US requirements for SPF and broad-spectrum testing, product stability, and labeling. With those considerations in mind, Kwon expects Round Lab to release its own bemotrizinol sunscreen sometime in 2027.

A sunscreen is only as useful as a person’s willingness to wear it consistently. Bemotrizinol’s ability to protect against UV damage is important, but its potential to make formulas lighter, less greasy, and more comfortable could be just as consequential to get people to implement it in their everyday skincare routines.

“One of the strengths of Korean sun care is how naturally it has built sun protection into the everyday skincare experience,” Kwon says. “For people to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it when needed, the way it feels matters as much as how well it protects.”

But better filters alone won’t transform American sun care. The real breakthrough will be sunscreens that people actually enjoy wearing—and, as a result, are more likely to apply generously and reapply throughout the day, a key step to ensuring its effectiveness.

Charlotte Palermino, cofounder and chief brand officer of skincare brand Dieux, has been an advocate for easier sunscreen filter approvals ever since she tried her first Japanese sunscreen, Biore UV, a decade ago. She realized sunscreen could stave off skin issues after her dermatologist told her that her hyperpigmentation had been the result of failing to use sun protection. In the years since she has publicly pushed for regulatory reform. She’s hesitant to put an estimated release date on Dieux’s upcoming BEMT-centric sunscreen, simply because the brand is dialed in to ensure its able to deliver a quality, wearable product.

“We’ve gone through this with [Dieux’s] SkinMercy, which is an OTC colloidal oatmeal cream, but for sunscreen, the stability of your sunscreen is so fucking important,” she says. “If my sunscreen separates or if it’s not at that stated SPF 50, if that degrades at all with broad spectrum protection, I would be mortified.”

Palerimo cites brands like Korea’s Beauty of Joseon, which is more popular in the US than in its home country, as evidence that Americans have long been on the hunt for better sunscreen. And though BEMT is a step forward, we still have a way to go. Board-certified dermatologist Jane Yoo has been lobbying Congress to get new sunscreen filters approved for the US and is tracking the FDA’s progress in making those approvals. Currently there are seven other filters—bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane, octyl triazone, amiloxate, diethylhexyl butamido triazone iscotrizinol, ecamsule, and enzacamene—under the agency’s Time and Extent Application (TEA) pipeline. Those filters are part of the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act meant to speed up the process of determining if ingredients are Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective, or GRASE. But here we are 12 years later, and we’re still waiting for their approval.

“A good analogy is we’ve been making sunscreens with both of our hands tied behind our backs,” Palermino says. “We’ve now had one hand released. I would like both hands released.”

The Alleyoop Pen Pal 4-in-1 Touch-Up Pen comes in three different variations (though they all have black eyeliner and champagne highlighter): In a Rouge, which is made for light skin tones and has taupe brow pencil and nude pink lip liner; Make a Mauve, meant for medium skin tones, which features dark brown brow pencil and mauve lip liner; and Berry Busy, a deeper option that has berry lip liner and dark brown brow pencil. The eyeliner is particularly easy to blend if you’re after a smoky, smudged-out look, but as someone who rarely leaves the house without a little wing, I’m pleased to find that I can still achieve a precise flick with the help of a straight-edged piece of card. Suffice it to say, the next time I’m jet-setting somewhere, I’m leaving my assortment of pencils behind and making room for this multitasking Alleyoop pen instead.”

“The only way I can describe this pen is that it is an all-in-one makeup product designed for the girl on the go (a.k.a. me).
