And no, I'm not over the nostalgia for the pen, either.”

“I love the idea of having an all-in-one tool I can just throw in my purse or bag on days when I’m not sure if I want to wear makeup or not. In fact, I might get a second one of these pens to just leave at my desk.”

#6664. BA's Best Rice Krispies Treats

Perhaps the most nostalgic of all recipes, a classic Rice Krispies treat is hard to beat. There’s just something about the crisp yet gooey texture that can’t be replicated. While the classic back-of-box recipe is a guaranteed winner, we thought it was high time to give the original a run for its money. Introducing our new favorite way to make Rice Krispies treats, with a few small (but dramatic) tweaks to the original formula. For starters, this version increases the butter and browns it, adding a subtle nutty flavor. From there, the marshmallows are split in two: The first set gets fully melted into the butter along with salt and vanilla, while the remaining set gets folded in along with the cereal so you get pockets of stretchy marshmallow throughout. While seemingly insignificant, these small changes make for a Rice Krispies treat that’s perfectly pullable, delightfully sweet yet salty, and just a touch more exciting than the classic.

Read More: The Only Type of Marshmallows I’ll Use for Rice Krispies Treats

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Lightly coat a 13x9" baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray and line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on long sides. Cook ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat, stirring constantly, until butter foams, then darkens to a light amber, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and immediately add one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and quickly stir until marshmallows are melted.

Add remaining one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows and 9 cups Rice Krispies or other puffed rice cereal to pot and mix until cereal is completely coated in melted marshmallow mixture and last addition of marshmallows is melted slightly. Working quickly, transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer. (Don’t press too hard.) Let sit at least 1 hour before cutting into squares.

Do Ahead: Rice Krispies treats can be made 2 days ahead. Store tightly covered at room temperature.

#6660. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6659. Boyedoe Lagos Spring 2027

Across several African nations, fashion plays a significant part in shaping ceremonial attire. Ghanaian designer David Kusi Boyedoe is reimagining how heritage and culture can exist in today’s world. For spring 2027, he was heavily influenced by the Asante Kingdom, a Ghanaian ethnic group, and their dynamic relationship between an Asante King and the Asante man. “It’s also a return to our ideology, which is about going back and restoring, and making known our silhouettes,” he said. With this collection, titled ‘Oath’ (or ‘Ntam’ in Twi, a Ghanaian language), Boyedoe is swearing a pledge to his craft.

Often, there’s a monolithic perception of African fashion: it’s either experimental and bold or lacking commerciality to the Western world. But there’s a cohort of African designers that are offering a counter perspective, and Boyedoe is one of them. “Instead of creating a spectacle, I’m focused on designs that sell,” he said. Even though this collection is more commercially-driven and wearable, there’s still an interesting story rooted in culture, community, and craftsmanship—particularly as the majority of his pieces are handmade by local artisans in Ghana.

Overall, this collection wasn’t about spectacle. Upcycled denim, sourced from textile waste dumped in Ghana, was reworked into his signature patchwork design. Standout looks included a mini patchwork dress and a pair of barrel jeans paired with an off-white blazer. The denim was another avenue into accessories in the form of medium-sized patchwork bags. Boyedoe also introduced a new earthy color palette in silhouettes like an ivory coat and a moss green suit.

#6656. 11 Best Men's Dress Shirts 2026, According to GQ Editors

Even if your closet is ninety percent fleece, the best men's dress shirts are non-negotiables. At some point, you’ll face an occasion that requires one—a laid-back wedding, a high-stakes job interview, a weirdly formal middle-school piano recital. But the right dress shirt won’t just save you in a pinch or help you sneak past upper management at your new corporate gig. (Especially if said corporate gig is working at GQ.)

Because the superlative versions of the style aren’t simply dress shirts—or, at least, not exclusively dress shirts. Buy one equipped with the right fit, details, and fabrics, and even the most formal of the bunch can kick it in less stuffy environments without eliciting snickers. We’re on-the-record fans of throwing one on with a groovy tie and crisp trousers, but toss a dress shirt over a graphic tee and baggy shorts, and suddenly, your otherwise schlubby fit looks exponentially more considered—and exponentially more stylish.

For starters, polos aren’t dress shirts just because they have a collar. We know, we know—finding the line between casual shirts and formal shirts is hard. Then there’s fabric, little details like cuffs, plackets, and color. And on top of all that, “the perfect fit” is so subjective. Take a deetp breath. We’ve got you. We’ve done the dirty work, buttoned more buttons than we thought was possible, aggregated a heap of our favorites, and wore ‘em every which way possible to determine, once and for all, the absolute best dress shirts for men.

We’ve wholeheartedly recommended J.Crew’s Bowery dress shirts for a long time. But it was up until just recently that the revered preppy label quietly released a new button-up that we had to do some internal reckoning. The Slim Portuguese cotton Oxford dress shirt doesn’t enjoy the distinction of being named after a New York City street (e.g. the Ludlow suit, or the 770 jeans). But don’t let the straight-forward, flavorless nomenclature fool you. Let’s start with the obvious: the fabric. It’s an all-cotton Oxford cloth woven exclusively for J.Crew by the respected Portuguese mill, Solemos. It’s smooth and luxurious with an elegant drape. Plus, the thicker yarns of an Oxford cloth makes it versatile enough for less formal occasions when you want to wear it with a pair of jeans, untucked, even.

It gets better from there. The shirt is a tastefully trimmed down to a silhouette that’s not skin-tight nor 2010s #menswear slim, but svelte enough to look clean without a blazer. But the real star of the show is that 10-out-of-10 collar. Most of J.Crew’s shirts are designed with wimpier collars that are likely, for better or worse, a product of those aforementioned #menswear times. This newcomer, however, extends it enough to a more classic size that bridges the blazer-collar gap so it sits neatly below a jacket lapel. That larger collar means it’s more proportional when paired with a tie.

We’re not a part of J.Crew’s internal meetings, but if anyone there is reading this, we think this needs to be expanded into more fabrics, colorways, and silhouettes—perhaps, it should even be dubbed with a new name.

If it comes as any surprise that Uniqlo sells one of the best bang-for-your-buck dress shirts on the market, you’re likely new to GQ Recommends—and the Japanese retailer’s assortment of eminently affordable men’s clothing staples. Unlike its Calvin Klein counterpart, Uniqlo’s riff on the genre isn’t available with the added benefit of Prime shipping, but what you get instead is a dress shirt that’s worth exponentially more than what you pay for.

You might only go to Uniqlo for the basics—tees, underwear, socks, maybe a hoodie. So I'd understand if you thought dress shirts were too refined a category for Uniqlo to be any good. But every I time I encounter a dress shirt from the Japanese retailer, I'm reminded of just how surprisingly solid its fits and construction are. Unlike most of its price-conscious competition, Uniqlo’s dress shirt is made from 100% long-staple cotton with absolutely zero stretch involved. While you might think of a little elastane as a good thing, generally speaking, it tends to mean that corners were cut. Plus, if a dress shirt fits well, you won't need any stretch.

The fabric is treated for wrinkle resistance, which is great if you're the kind of guy who has a “clothes chair”. But there's a funny sort of sheen that comes with wrinkle-resistant shirts that can be off-putting. That said, the details redeem it completely: no sloppy stitching, exposed seams, or wimpy collars here. Perhaps most crucially, the slim fit isn’t so svelte that you’ll look like you got dressed in 2010.

Both our overall pick and budget pick are solid options no matter your budget or snobbery. But if you're ready to graduate or just feeling like skipping ahead to the finer things, Todd Snyder's line of in-house shirting is where we'd point you. A great dress shirt starts with great fabric and Mr. Snyder's collection is full of top-notch poplins, twills, and broadcloths sourced from Thomas Mason, a revered mill that's been around since 1796 and have been the go-to for grail shirtmakers like Turnbull & Asser, not to mention the Royal family.

In the hands of American menswear nobility, the fabrics are given that distinct yet trend-averse Todd Snyder flavor. It's cut with a tastefully slim silhouette that's not Slimane-skinny, but not what your dad thinks of as skinny, either. The back features comfy side pleats, which are sewn into a split yoke (a fairly uncommon, but appreciated detail for the menswear nerds). Fine stitching and single-needle construction throughout, the shirt is built with a ton of delectable details for stylishly discerning, but what we love most is the extended collar. It's a detail that feels refreshing but also recalls shirts from the 1930s, arguably a golden age for tailoring in the States.

This beauty will run you a bit over $200, which ain't nothing. But that's a resonable sum compared to the heritage shirtmakers whose reputations have been built on shirting alone. Often, their shirts can cost you as much as your car's mortgage. That said, Todd Snyder's will get you like, 90% of the way there for a third of the price.

Got a last-minute invite to a swanky event and need a dress shirt ASAP? Not to fear, Amazon is here (and there, and pretty much everywhere). Calvin Klein’s no-frills slim fit shirt is cut from high-quality cotton that’s just a tad more stretchy than our overall pick, and comes equipped with plenty of next-gen specs its counterparts eschew—including moisture-wicking properties to keep you cool and a non-iron coating to keep it looking crisp. (You’re short on time, right?) Mercifully, the added spandex offers a little give without making the shirt look too shiny.

Throw it over your finest chinos or the dress pants you impulsively splurged on or wear it with jeans on a relaxed Friday in the office. Even if you bought it at the eleventh hour, it won’t take long for it to supplant the pricier competition.

When you’re rolling with the movers and shakers of the world, you need a dress shirt that can keep up. And that’s exactly what the vaunted Parisian chemise-makers at Charvet specialize in, to the delight of royalty both literal (countless French kings) and cultural (Sofia Coppola is a well-known fan). This breezy cotton number is no exception: It’s cut on the looser side and features an extremely classy double cuff for when you're ready to break out the cufflinks you inherited from your old man. Even with the tres formale flourishes, though, we wouldn't shy away from rocking it in a more casual context. When you slip on this sucker, you don’t need to meet with the boss—you are the boss.

“Charvet does not fuck around,” Grossman says bluntly. There’s no shortage of reasons why it remains the first name in old-world dress shirts—and its centuries of pedigree barely cracks the top five. Sure, the brand has outfitted kings, presidents, and titans of industry in equal number, but its core value proposition comes down to one exceedingly simple principle: uncompromising quality. Every dress shirt is still made by hand in Charvet’s wood-paneled Parisian townhouse, which is worth the cost of a flight to visit, Grossman notes.

If you’re not quite ready to drop half a grand on a dress shirt your grandkids will fight over, he also recommends a more wallet-friendly hack: These days, Charvet’s shirts are all over the vintage market, and “you can reliably score one for a lot less than retail”.

Proper Cloth’s been an open secret to menswear heads for years thanks to its surprisingly granular made-to-order service which offers a wide range of custom options from fabric to design details to sizing. Beyond the near-bespoke service, Proper Cloth’s quality will turn the heads of the keen-eyed tailoring nerds. 80s two-ply pinpoint fabric made from American Supima cotton, split yoke construction, and a handsome semi spread collar all come together for one of the best dress shirts you can get for the price.

One of the most compelling arguments we’ve seen in favor of dressing up right now comes straight from Paris, where Husbands outfits its worldly clientele in exquisite dress shirts exactly like this, a masterclass in retro ‘70s swagger so good it clinched a spot in GQ’s inaugural All-Stars class. It looks rad unbuttoned to the navel, and even groovier with a hefty foulard tie.

One of the best things about a cutaway collar? It gives you more room for a declaratively large tie knot.

The J.Crew pick up top is incredible. But it's slim. This Ludlow dress shirt has all the same reliability, but is also cut to a fuller shape.

Given the brand’s stellar reputation in the tailoring place, it shouldn’t come as a shock that Sid Mashburn hawks a grip of bang-up dress shirts, too. This bengal stripe number is a tried-and-true riff on a traditional office-ready pattern, but the spread collar and Goldilocks cut imbue it with Mahsburn’s signature Southern charm—and yank it firmly into 2025.

While this nicely-priced shirt does also come in white, it's also a good reminder that dress shirts can still have some edge, too.

As with any garment, “good” is subjective—but as a general rule of thumb, it comes down to three crucial factors: fabric, construction, and fit. Men’s dress shirts are no different. Michael Hill, Creative Director of Drake’s says, “Versatility is important. Customers need to understand fabric and context. For instance, Oxford cotton is going to be more versatile than poplin, which is typically a bit more formal.” The fabric will help dictate the occasion (or the other way around?). There are so many at your disposal from herringbone to end-on-end to pinpoint, not to mention stripes to plaids. So if you’re not sure, ask the sales staff.

Hill also emphasizes that fit is essential to a good dress shirt and to pay attention to the details like “The way the collar sits on your neck and against the body of the shirt. Does it stay tucked in throughout the day? How do the cuffs sit against the wrist?”

He goes on to give this absolute, “Great dress shirts are never made from synthetic or stretch fabrics.” The majority of good dress shirts eschew synthetic materials in favor of natural long-staple cotton, woven tightly for extra durability. Cotton, of course, is not a prerequisite—but almost every single great dress shirt we’ve swaddled our torsos in has been made from some riff on the fabric, from poplin to pinpoint Oxford cloth.

Other reliable indicators of quality shirts? Telltale details like French or felled seams, which are sleeker and more durable; mother of pearl buttons; and a denser or finer stitch count, usually commensurate with the amount of craftsmanship involved. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth also notes to look out for less common details like reinforced shirt tail gussets, a split yoke, tight and straight stitching, and emphasizes the importance of buttons. “Are the buttons shanked so they won’t come loose? Are the buttons a durable enough material that can withstand your cleaners repeatedly?” These small details reveal whether a shirtmaker is paying close attention.

One unique difference between dress shirts and other garments comes down to the collar. Skerritt says the collar “often has the largest impact on how the shirt makes you look.” That’s because it frames your face and interacts with directly with your suit jacket and its lapels—no small job for a garment. While Skerritt advises to look for fusing (the way that the collar is attached or glued to its interlining) that’s crisp, and a collar that stands up well around the neck, ultimately it “should look natural and effortless. The end result should be [that] you like how it makes you feel in the way that you like to dress.”

As any menswear wonk will tell you, dress shirts boast no shortage of nuances. So in the name of brevity (and general wonk-avoidance), we compiled a handy-dandy glossary to the terms you’ll encounter most often. As a rule of thumb, the less adornment a dress shirt has, the more formal it is.

Like all of menswear, collars are susceptible to the whims of the trend cycle, swelling and shrinking with any given era’s silhouettes du jour. Collar sizes are prone to change, too (see: the massive collars of the power-suited ‘80s; the ultra-shrunken collars of the indie-sleaze 2010s). These are the three you should know.

Cuffs are the small pieces of additional fabric at the end of the shirt sleeve; they're often constructed with stiffer linings to give them structure and thoroughly cover your wrists. These are the two you should know.

Plackets are the strip of fabric that runs down the front of the shirt, designed to be fastened with buttons, snaps, or zippers. (When it comes to dress shirts, you’ll almost always encounter the former.) These are the three you should know.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6655. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6653. Nobody Wants to Have a Baby Boy Anymore

It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, and a new ritual was born.

Nearly 20 years later, we all know the drill. If it isn’t a cake, it’s a balloon or a cannon. Friends and family gather. Someone counts down; something explodes in blue or pink; the parents-to-be hug; a grandparent enters the frame looking thrilled and slightly confused. And, of course, there’s a camera rolling, meaning my daughter could have in theory earned her first “like” long before she drew her first breath.

For the first time in a century, nearly less than half of parents are circumcising their newborns. New dad Kevin Lincoln investigates how America’s favorite elective surgery became as debated as childhood vaccines—and considers his own decision.

The gender reveal has evolved from a modest party trick into a full-blown genre of internet spectacle, complete with its own newborn industrial complex. Private ultrasound companies now sell “gender-reveal experiences,” with rooms that glow pink or blue and teddy bears containing recordings of an unborn baby’s heartbeat. Online, the reveals have become more elaborate: smoke bombs, pyrotechnics (one of which started a wildfire in South California in 2020), choreographed dances, skydivers and, in one particularly memorable case, a Louisiana alligator called Sally biting through a blue jelly watermelon.

But the spectacle has moved on. A new kind of gender-reveal video is becoming a genre of its own, one in which a particular reaction is the main event. A recent compilation racked up 33 million views and three million likes on TikTok. Expecting couples do not scream with delight when the color appears. They scream in horror. They collapse and cry. The reason is nearly always the same: it’s blue. They’re having a boy.

What looks like internet absurdity may actually point to something much bigger. Last year, The Economist published data showing that in mostly higher-income countries, the centuries-old preference for sons is starting to reverse. And in some countries, the data shows that opinion has fully flipped: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Portugal and the Czech Republic are showing evidence of a preference for girls.

In the US, the same trend appears among adoptive parents. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, prospective parents were willing to pay an average $16,000 more for a girl than a boy. Among couples having IVF in the US—where, unlike the UK, sex selection is legal— leading clinics have reported that 75–80% of patients want a girl.

This is a big demographic plot twist. On one hand, it’s what progress looks like. For most of human history, boys have been the prize. They inherited the family name and property. They were expected to earn money and carry the family line into the future. Girls, in turn, were generally expected to marry out or care for relatives.

In the worst cases, the preference for sons has had lethal consequences. In China, where a one-child policy enforced by the government lasted 35 years, and in India, sex-selective abortion and the killing or abandonment of female babies has led to generations with far more boys than girls. Misogynist discrimination has been so pervasive that in 1990, the Nobel Prize–winning economist Amartya Sen estimated that more than 100 million women were “missing” from world history. (Researchers have since questioned the precise figure and methodology, but the point still stands.)

But there is another, stranger side to the reversal. You don’t have to spend long reading the 20,000-plus comments beneath a viral gender-reveal video to realize that some of this isn’t simply about girls finally being valued properly. There is a growing and increasingly open distaste for boys—a sense that they are inherently problematic, undesirable by default.

Having a son, in certain corners of modern parenthood, has become unfashionable. A curious society might ask itself why this is—and where it might lead.

Ruth Whippman is the mother of three boys. She grew up in England but now lives in America, in what she describes as a “progressive area of the country [with] very progressive school districts”. As she writes in her 2024 book, BoyMom, friends and neighbors kept saying versions of the same thing: “I hope for your sake this one is a girl.”

“We were a year into the [first] Trump presidency,” she tells me. “There were incels on the news. There was just this huge backlash against toxic masculinity. So it wasn’t even just a sense of, ‘Oh, boys, their clothes aren’t as nice; you don’t get to play Barbies.’ It was this sense that boys are actively toxic and harmful.”

My son and I were calling to each other across a great distance, a distance that I was aware might never close.

When Whippman’s first son was due, she had the standard worries about raising a child of the opposite sex. Would they have enough in common? Would she know how to navigate experiences she hadn’t had? As a lifelong feminist, she tells me, the additional sense of cultural disapproval made everything worse. “It was really horrible, because nobody likes to be pitied,” she says. “Nobody likes to think that their children are second best. But I think it played into something in me as well, if I’m totally honest. I had my own fears and feelings about [having boys], and hearing everybody else’s reaction just made it much worse.”

Nearly a decade on from #MeToo, with Donald Trump back in the White House and male chauvinism metastasizing across the internet, it’s unusual to hear the word “masculinity” without the word “toxic” prefacing it. So parents can end up feeling—even if they’re guilty about it—that having a son is more complicated than it was for previous generations.

“When you hear about boys at the moment, at best, they’re this underachieving lunk who won’t go to college, is doing badly at school and will fail to launch,” says Whippman. “And at worst, he’s deep in the manosphere, commanding his AI girlfriend to let him choke her, or whatever. It gets to this wider consumerisation of parenthood. [The idea that] girls are better consumer products, in a way—which is a terrible, terrible way to talk about human beings.”

I’d be lying if I said it hadn’t crossed my mind, when I discovered I was having a daughter, that if I could raise her to be a confident, secure, kick-ass girl, I’d win the approval of the types of circle I move in. “Girl dads” who let daughters paint their nails are the subject of endless kind TikTok videos.

Parents of boys, not so much. Whippman, who has heard more and more fathers say they would prefer daughters, recognizes the problem. “Parenting a son is almost seen as a harm reduction project, rather than anything empowering,” she says. “That’s really at odds with our modern parenting culture, which is about encouraging [our kids] to reach for the stars and be happy and access all the world has to offer.”

And like everything else in 2026, the random, happy event of your unborn child’s sex can somehow thrust you into the us-versus-them culture war. “In the States and in the UK, there’s a sense that if you are on the progressive left, you are on the side of girls and women… any time you’re defending boys and men, it has this sniff of something right-wing, or being a bad actor,” says Whippman. “That’s a really hard thing to hold as a progressive, feminist parent of a son.”

There are other theories for why parents in Western countries, in particular, are increasingly downbeat about having boys. Millennials are having fewer children than any generation in history, and we’re doing it later in life. In other words, by the time it happens, we’re already exhausted. And boys are often perceived as more work, especially when they’re little: more physical, and harder to keep occupied and under control.

Lara Miller has been a midwife for more than 20 years. She uses social media to demystify pregnancy and childbirth. She thinks there is some truth to the idea that older parents may be wary of boys. “When you see older people having babies, they tend to be more controlling about everything to do with it,” she says. “I say this without judgment—I was an older mum myself—but you become used to doing things your own way and to your own routines.”

Of course, it would be silly to assume every girl will be content quietly coloring in while every boy spends his childhood trailing dog shit through the house. But according to Alex Trippier, a kids’ club leader who runs the social media account Be A Happier Parent, there can be real differences in behavior. “You get testosterone surges around age two, which I really see with the kids that I look after in my groups,” he says. “All of a sudden the boys come in and they’re going crazy. Parents who are on the quieter side can be overwhelmed by the sheer energy. Some people insist this is all nonsense, and [boys being more boisterous] is completely socialized. I think it’s a mixture of both. You’ve got that developmental layer going on, and you’ve got all the socialization on top of it.”

Trippier, who has two boys and a girl, thinks culture has shifted. Parents have always worried about teenage girls. But now, they have a whole new list of concerns for boys: porn, gaming addiction, exam results, algorithms. “There are all these fears we have for our sons, this kind of moral anxiety about the impossibility of raising good men,” he says.

In 2024, Zach Baron documented his long journey to fatherhood via IVF in GQ. Now, he reports on the mind-altering chaos (and occasional brilliance) of life with two walking, talking young boys.

Miller, who had similar feelings when she was pregnant but is now the happy mother of two sons, thinks there’s another factor: Schools aren’t always very good at accommodating boys. “We have changed as a society and we’re not as accepting of boys,” she says. “Boys don’t tend to fit the school model. You get worse reports. [Our school] gives the boys set days to be allowed to kick a football. Well, you don’t remember that at school, do you?”

She recalls being summoned by a headmaster after her son made a gun sign with his fingers. “The girls do better at school,” she says. “They’ve read 20 books; my boys have only read two. The teacher’s gone, ‘Well, if you buy a football magazine, do you think they’d read that?’ You’re like, ‘Oh, fuck off. Just fuck off.’”

There’s something else unusual about today’s parents, beyond grappling with the manosphere and Parkrun injuries. We’re the most psychologically literate generation to have ever lived. If we haven’t done therapy ourselves, we’re at least sufficiently fluent in the language of therapy to take a stab at self-reflection (or, as Boomer parents might call it, self-absorption). We know about childhood trauma. We know about attachment styles. We know that our parents’ behavior has consequences. We know that our childhoods don’t simply disappear when we become adults. It gives us an enormous number of things to worry about.

One of the most interesting conversations I’ve had on this subject is with a colleague who is expecting a son. He’s delighted now, but initially, the prospect of having a boy unnerved him—as it did me, before I knew the sex of my baby. We both agreed this probably came from remembering difficult experiences with our own fathers, and being afraid of repeating them. For me, it may have gone a step further. The idea of having a son scared me because I had a pretty broken relationship with myself.

Dr. Chrissy Jayarajah is a psychiatrist and the author of the world’s only academic paper on “gender disappointment.” She’s quick to point out that the term is not a clinical diagnosis, but what you might call a “known phenomenon” (particularly on TikTok, where thousands of videos are tagged with it).

“Something I always say is that becoming a parent will undoubtedly make you reflect on the way that you were parented,” she says. “Whether it was a good relationship, a bad relationship, an indifferent relationship or a non-existent relationship—they all play a part. An absent father is still very present in your mind. We are more psychologically minded and reflective compared with, maybe, the generation before. But I also think we don’t know what to do with that reflection.”

This can manifest in different ways, explains Jayarajah. “Working predominantly with mothers, I would say they fall into two camps,” she says. “They either want to emulate exactly how their mother was, from recreating those childhood memories, making those family favorite meals on a Sunday, and so on. Or they’re: ‘Oh my God, I’m turning into my mother.’”

That can produce powerful feelings about your baby’s sex. “We see that with women who have experienced abuse of some kind,” says Jayarajah. “Some absolutely do not want to have a girl, because they don’t want their daughter to experience what they went through. On the other hand, I have had women who say, ‘No, I definitely want a girl. I don’t want to have a son,’ because a son [would remind] them of the perpetrator.”

The sex of your baby, in other words, can become a vessel for all sorts of fears that existed long before the baby did. Then, there’s the demographic problem. There just aren’t enough babies. A rapid collapse in birth rates and fertility is playing out across the world. In 1990, global fertility was about 3.3 children per woman. Today it is around 2.2 to 2.3. More than half the countries in the world are already below “replacement level.”

The consequences will be huge. Labor shortages. Pressure on pensions. Rising social and healthcare costs. Less of the innovation and forward momentum traditionally associated with younger populations. In that context, favoring one sex over the other seems beyond counterproductive.

Maybe we are retreating into old, narrow assumptions. “We’ve never thought about gender more as a society than we do at this present day,” says Jayarajah. “Ideas about gender are in our face all day long. There was no such thing as a gender reveal party 20 years ago, let alone putting it online. What’s happening, in my opinion, is gender essentialism. This sexist idea of what it means to be a man, what it means to be a woman, is playing out in what we expect for our children.”

The following week, I saw this in action. I took my 19-month-old daughter to a soft-play morning, where she likes to roll around on the multicolored shapes and go down the slide on my lap. A few minutes after we arrived, I heard a scream. “Aaaargh!”

At one end of the ball pit, a little boy was staring at his own reflection in a mirror. “Aaaargh!” he went again, hammering his fists against the perspex and making the entire frame shake. A few feet away, my daughter watched him quietly. I made a mental note to keep them as far apart as possible.

The boy’s parents were nearby, deep in conversation. They seemed oblivious, or perhaps simply immune, to their son’s King Kong routine. A dozen judgmental thoughts zipped through my head. Why aren’t you keeping a closer eye on him? What kind of irresponsible shit are you pulling at home for him to do this? If he harms her, I swear to God…

I took a sip of my coffee, scrolled through my phone, then turned around, ready to rescue my sweet, innocent little girl. The boy who had been screaming a moment ago was now shyly handing her a dumper truck with a missing wheel. She closed her eyes, grinned, and took it with both hands.

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “For Centuries, Everyone Wanted Boys. Now, Not So Much”

#6650. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6649. Fruché Lagos Spring 2027

It was an exciting summer for Frank Aghuno, founder and creative director of Fruche. After winning Berlin Fashion Week’s contemporary prize, Aghuno travelled some 3,000 miles to the German capital and held his first international showcase. Still riding that high, the Lagos-based designer was eager to bring the collection home and present it to his Nigerian audience.

This collection asked us to embrace our natural quirks and imperfections. At times, that took on a literal meaning; “handwork can be imperfect in its natural state,” he said, be it naturally occurring holes in the wood carved beads or imperfections from dyeing. “There are quirks everywhere, from the perfectly styled looks to the looks that are more twisted and knotted,” he said.

Inspired by Nigerian boarding school uniforms, gingham featured heavily throughout the collection and came in several iterations, including cotton gingham; aso oke (a Nigerian textile) gingham; beaded gingham; and adire gingham, a traditional resist-dyeing technique. While the silhouettes felt contemporary, traditional crafting techniques remained a key component. From the fabric to the local wood carving, Aghuno was keen to collaborate with artisans based in Nigeria. The cotton used was sourced from Katsina and milled in Nigeria. “Everything is sourced here, and every look was made around the country,” he said, adding that he searched high and low for the right team to help develop the collection (including discovering craftsmen on TikTok). “It just goes to show the richness of our culture and the work we are doing today,” he said.

Standout looks included a satin dress and shirt featuring hand-painted artwork by Aghuno’s twin brother Dricky, an artist based between Lagos and London. At the show’s end, we heard the final look before it appeared on the runway. A model wearing an outfit made out of wood-carved shells walked out as the music drew to a close. The crowd fell quiet as they perched up in their seats and listened closely to the soothing sound of the beads brushing against each other. It was the first time I’ve heard Lagos that silent.

#6645. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6644. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed. Braiding is a perfect example: it is a process that has not materially changed in thousands of years, despite being one of the most popular hairstyles for millions of Americans and a significant part of the $270 billion salon services industry,” said Ohanian. “Yinka has introduced a novel technology to a traditionally manual and highly specialized professional service.”

Company description: L’Oréal Group has taken a stake in Indian personal care company Innovist. (Vogue Business reported on speculations back in March.) The company has a successful portfolio that includes Indian haircare brand Bare Anatomy, skincare brands Chemist at Play and Sunscoop, and bodycare brand Vinci Botanicals. The company was founded in 2018 by Rohit Chawla, Sifat Khurana, and Vimal Bhola with a focus on science-first formulations, transparent ingredients, and in-house research and development.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L’Oréal Group (portfolio includes: Cerave, La Roche-Posay, Vichy, Armani Beauty, SkinCeuticals).

Investor comments: “Our investment in this innovative Indian startup is a clear testament to our unwavering commitment to expanding L’Oréal’s footprint in India,” CEO Nicolas Hieronimus said. “By bringing together the very best of L’Oréal’s global expertise with Innovist’s high-performing, science-led products and deep-rooted understanding of the Indian consumer, I believe we are poised to shape the future of beauty in this dynamic market.”

Company description: Remedy is a dermatologist-developed skincare brand founded by Dr. Muneeb Shah in March 2024. The brand’s products target skin concerns such as dark spots, dryness, fine lines, dullness, keratosis pilaris, and sensitive skin. Remedy is stocked on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Target, the latter of which it partnered with in December 2025. The Series A investment will support the skincare brand with its next phase of growth, including advancing clinical research, expanding its product categories, and improving inventory. Remedy also plans to strengthen its formulation, testing, and consumer education.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L Catterton (portfolio includes: Merit Beauty, Tula, Kopari, Elemis, Nutrafol, Intercos, Ex Nihilo).

Investor comments: “We seek to partner with exceptional founders building brands that will redefine categories, and we believe Remedy is uniquely modernizing dermatological skincare,” L Catterton partner Tehmina Haider said. “As both a clinician and a consumer educator, Dr. Shah has built a portfolio of simple, effective, and accessibly priced products that leverage advanced ingredient technologies to address real patient needs — and that is what will define the next generation of dermocosmetics. The brand’s rapid growth reflects deep consumer demand for affordable, clinically-grounded skincare, and we are thrilled to partner with the Remedy team on its next chapter.”

Company description: Bacchus is a London-based PR agency founded in 1998 by Anouschka Menzies and Charlotte Lurot, who currently lead the business alongside co-CEO Daize Washbourn. The agency specializes in luxury hospitality and culture, as well as in the prestige VIC and high-net-worth communities. With around 100 employees across seven offices (London, New York, Miami, LA, Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha), Bacchus generates annual sales of approximately $17 million. Its client portfolio includes Red Sea Global Residences, Six Senses, Auberge Resorts, the Victoria & Albert Museum, and Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer.

Funding and round: Acquisition, majority stake.

Investor(s): Mazarine Group (portfolio includes: La Mode en Images, the show producer of Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Gucci).

Investor comments: “There were several objectives [with this investment],” Mazarine founder Paul-Emmanuel Reiffers tells Vogue Business. “First, we needed to add a public relations and influence branch to our group. Second, it had to be large enough for us to develop and accelerate it. With Bacchus, we’re starting from a platform that’s already large enough to consolidate operations, grow further, and open an office in Paris in the short to medium-term. Third, the acquisition gives us seven offices at once, providing an established global network and strengthening our geographic footprint. We already had a presence in Dubai, but now we’re able to establish ourselves in Riyadh, which is important because the Middle East is about to rebound strongly. We’re also strengthening our position in the US by expanding our network from New York to LA and Miami, allowing us to serve clients more effectively.”

He continues: “Finally, the acquisition aligns with what we see as the luxury sectors of tomorrow: hospitality, real estate, and longevity. As luxury brands increasingly move into these areas, we are positioning ourselves to support their expansion. It also creates valuable synergies, allowing us to integrate Bacchus’s expertise and network of personalities, influencers, and guests into our events.”

Company description: Bella Hadid has been slowly growing her fragrance brand Orebella since its launch in 2024. Now, with Series A funding from Silas Capital, which has previously invested in beauty brands including Makeup by Mario, Oak Essentials and Ilia, she can scale the line further across categories and markets.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Silas Capital (portfolio includes: Makeup by Mario, YSE Beauty, Dôen).

Company description: NYC-based startup Vetir is pitching itself as an AI luxury shopping app that goes beyond discovery and transactions to act as “a system of record for the wardrobe” for high-value consumers. In practice, this is something of an AI stylist that learns from the data users share with the app, including existing closet items, shopping preferences, as well as their calendar, travel, and purchasing behavior. It’s also building out a business-to-business, CRM-type system for private stylists and luxury clienteling systems, aiming to bring “structure and continuity to what has traditionally been a fragmented, relationship-driven space”.

Funding and round: $5.5 million, Series A.

Investor(s): A consortium of investors across technology and luxury-adjacent family offices.

Company description: Ruka Hair was founded in 2021 by Tendai Moyo and Ugo Agbai, with the mission of supplying hair extensions that are safe, ethical, and good quality. The brand has now received $4.5 million in funding led by Henkel Ventures, the owner of Olaplex and Schwarzkopf. Ruka will be using the investment to scale its business, starting with the launch of US-based operations later this year. The brand has raised $10 million to date and is stocked at Selfridges.

Investor(s): Henkel Ventures, Freedom Trail Capital, Big Issue Invest, Backed VC, Dina Asher-Smith, Knut Alicke, Sophia Dennis, Didier Morais.

Investor comments: “Ruka Hair exemplifies what we look for: founders solving a real problem with genuine commitment, building through community rather than hype,” said Samyr Laine, co-founder and managing partner of Freedom Trail Capital. “Tendai and Ugo built this brand during one of the most challenging periods for consumer businesses, scaled through an authentic community, and are now pioneering biotech innovation that could reshape an entire category.”

Company description: Since founding Anomaly in 2021, Priyanka Chopra Jonas has scaled her haircare brand across North America, the UK, and the Middle East. In the US, the brand is stocked at Target, while in the UK, Superdrug is one of its biggest retailers. Chopra Jonas launched Anomaly with the aim to bring accessibly priced clean and vegan haircare products to the masses. The investment from Reliance will focus on scaling the brand further in India, alongside growing its international presence.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Reliance Retail (portfolio includes: Pahadi Local and Tira).

Investor comments: “Bringing Anomaly into our portfolio marks a strategic step in expanding our basket of new-age, high-growth beauty brands. Anomaly’s strong global positioning, clean formulation, and accessible pricing make it a compelling addition to our ecosystem,” said Isha Ambani, executive director of Reliance Retail Ventures Limited.

Company description: Luxury skincare brand 111Skin was co-founded by husband and wife duo, Dr. Yannis and Eva Alexandridis, in 2012. Their face masks have gone viral since, and in 2025, the brand received a minority investment from Kim Kardashian and Jay Sammons’s private equity firm Skky Partners to help fund its US expansion. Now, the Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) has invested a minority stake that will go toward science-driven innovation.

Funding and round: Minority investment, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): The Estée Lauder Companies (portfolio includes: Le Labo, Jo Malone London, Clinique, La Mer).

Investor comments: “Skincare is entering a new phase, shaped by the convergence of procedures, longevity, and beauty, as consumers increasingly seek products that deliver visible, treatment-inspired results,” said ELC president and CEO Stéphane de La Faverie. “111Skin exemplifies this shift, translating Dr. Alexandrides’s more than 35 years of surgical and aesthetic treatment experience into high-performance skincare inspired by in-clinic treatments and built on clinical insight, next-generation actives, powerful formulas, and proven efficacy.”

Company description: ICCF is a Shanghai and Paris-based premium fashion group that owns Chinese brand Icicle and French brand Carven (acquired in 2018). Kering has acquired a minority stake in ICCF to help develop the former label as part of Kering’s new House of Wonders initiative, which aims to build partnerships that equip emerging luxury houses with strong cultural relevance across markets, categories, and geographies. Icicle will use the funds to expand internationally and into new product categories.

Funding and round: Minority acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Kering (portfolio includes: Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta).

Investor comments: “This partnership brings together ICCF’s deep understanding of the Chinese luxury ecosystem and cultural landscape with Kering’s longstanding expertise in craftsmanship, operations, and brand development in Europe,” Kering said in a statement. “Through House of Wonders, Kering aims to build long-term value through a disciplined, partnership-driven approach, engaging with brands defined by a distinctive vision, deep authenticity, and global resonance potential.”

Icicle FW26. Photo: Benjamin Cremel/Getty Images

Company description: Grüns is a US-based supplement brand founded in 2023 by Chad Janis, best known for its greens superfood gummy supplement. The brand is digitally-native, with a strong community and a mixed distributed network across retail and direct-to-consumer. The acquisition signals Unilever’s push into the premium wellness category.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever (portfolio includes: Liquid I.V., Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice).

Investor comments: “As a leader and true innovator in the greens supplement category, what sets Grüns apart is its focused portfolio of science-backed products that people genuinely enjoy, trust, and consistently use,” Jostein Solheim, Unilever Wellbeing CEO, said. “This combination of efficacy and experience is powerful, and together we see a significant opportunity to scale the brand within our wellbeing business.”

Investor(s): Softbank, Andreessen Horowitz, D. E. Shaw Ventures, MGX, TPG, Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, BlackRock, Sequoia Capital, and more.

Company description: Whoop is a wearable tech company known for its fitness tracker that analyzes sleep, recovery, and performance.
